articles.title: Baby Bathing: A Guide to Safe and Soothing Baths
articles.excerpt: Step-by-step instructions for safely bathing your baby. Learn about water temperature, umbilical cord care, and how to turn bath time into a relaxing sleep routine.
articles.content:
Bathing your baby for the first time is one of the most exciting and memorable moments in the parenting journey. It's not just for hygiene, but also a wonderful opportunity to build a special bond with your baby and soothe them at the end of the day. A well-organized bath time can become a relaxing experience for some babies and an important part of their pre-sleep ritual.

However, this process can raise many questions, especially for new parents. What temperature is considered ideal? How often should you bathe them? How do you ensure safety? In this article, you will find answers to all these questions about baby bathing and learn how to make this process a pleasant and safe experience for both you and your baby.

The Soothing Effect of Bathing: Why Do Some Babies Love Baths?

Many babies enjoy being in warm water. This is due to the physical sensations created by the water. The contact of warm water with the body relaxes muscles and reduces tension. This can be especially beneficial for babies who are fussy during the day or suffer from gas colic. The gentle pressure of the water and its embrace provide them with a sense of security and comfort.

However, it's important to remember that every baby is different. Some babies may not immediately like the water. For them, undressing, temperature changes, or the sensation of being in water can be unusual and unsettling. If your baby cries or is uncomfortable during bath time, keep the process short and try to soothe them. With time and patience, most babies get used to taking baths and even start to enjoy them.

Bath Preparation: Safety Comes First

It is very important to prepare in advance to make the baby bathing process smooth and safe. Make sure everything is within reach before putting the baby in the water, as the baby should not be left unsupervised in the bath for even a second.

  1. Prepare All Supplies: Prepare items in advance such as a baby bathtub, 2 clean towels (one for padding, the other for drying), a clean diaper, clothes, fragrance-free and hypoallergenic baby soap/shampoo (if you will be using it), and a bath thermometer.
  2. Room Temperature: Prepare a comfortable and warm environment where the baby won't get cold; there is no mandatory exact degree for everyone. Keep the bath short, protect from drafts and overheating.
  3. Adjust Water Temperature Correctly: This is one of the most important points. The ideal water temperature should be close to the baby's body temperature, which is approximately 37°C. After pouring water into the tub, mix it with your hand to ensure the heat is evenly distributed. Using a special bath thermometer is the most reliable method to check the temperature. If you don't have a thermometer, you can check the water temperature with the inside of your wrist or elbow – the water should feel pleasantly warm, not hot.
  4. First Bath Time: The World Health Organization recommends delaying the first bath for at least 24 hours after birth, unless there is a medical necessity, to allow the baby to regulate its body temperature and benefit from the natural protective layer of its skin.

Step-by-Step Bathing Process and Important Rules

Once preparations are complete, you can begin the bathing process. Being calm and confident will also have a positive effect on your baby.

  • Constant Supervision: Never leave the baby alone in the bath, even for a moment, or under the supervision of another child. One hand should always be on the baby. Bath seats do not make the baby safe; do not rely on them.
  • Correct Hold: Gently place the baby in the water. Support their head and neck by placing one arm under their back, and use your other hand to wash them.
  • Umbilical Cord Care: If the umbilical cord has not yet fallen off, follow your doctor's advice. Many experts recommend sponge baths (wiping the body with a damp cloth) instead of full immersion to keep the umbilical cord dry. If the umbilical cord accidentally gets wet, gently dry it with a soft, clean cloth after the bath.
  • Washing Sequence: Wash the baby from top to bottom, starting from the cleanest areas. First, wipe their face with cotton soaked only in warm water. Then wash their head (if you are using shampoo), then their body, and finally the diaper area. Make sure to thoroughly clean between skin folds (armpits, neck, groin).
  • Keep the Process Short: Especially in the first months, try not to extend bath time beyond 5-10 minutes. The baby's body can cool down quickly. If the baby shows signs of discomfort or gets cold, end the bath immediately.
  • Drying and Dressing: Remove the baby from the water and immediately wrap them in a hooded or regular towel. Gently pat their skin dry without rubbing. If there is skin dryness, you can use a fragrance-free, baby-appropriate moisturizer with your doctor's advice. Then put on a clean diaper and clothes.

Turning Bath Time into a Soothing Pre-Sleep Ritual

A consistently repeated evening routine helps the baby understand that bedtime is approaching. A soothing bath can be a perfect part of this routine. The gradual decrease in the baby's body temperature after coming out of warm water is a natural signal that facilitates falling asleep.

An effective pre-sleep routine might look like this: Bath → Gentle Massage → Pajamas → Feeding → Story/Lullaby → Sleep. Avoid bathing the baby immediately after feeding, as this can cause discomfort. It is more appropriate to bathe them some time before or after feeding. After placing your baby in their bed after the bath, make sure they are lying on their back.

When to Contact a Doctor?

While bathing is usually a safe process, some symptoms require medical advice. It is important to contact your doctor in the following cases:

  • Fever of 3°C or higher in a baby younger than 38 months: This situation requires immediate medical attention.
  • Redness, swelling, pus, or a strong unpleasant odor around the umbilical cord: These could be signs of infection.
  • Unusual rashes, severe redness, or prolonged dryness on the skin: This could indicate an allergy, eczema, or another skin problem.
  • If the baby cries excessively every time they are bathed and cannot be soothed: It may be helpful to talk to a doctor to clarify if there is another underlying cause.

Keep Anacan-Related Notes in One Place

Remembering daily details can be exhausting. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Sleep history: Track the daily rhythm by recording the start and end of sleep with a timer. The app does not monitor breathing during sleep and does not replace safe sleep guidelines.
  • Diaper logs: Record the time of wet, soiled, and mixed diapers. This information can help the doctor assess feeding, but it does not diagnose dehydration or other illnesses on its own.

It is possible to share feeding, sleep, and diaper logs in the Doctor's Report. Available entry and Premium terms for tools apply. Do not delay medical attention to write a note in the app for urgent symptoms.

faq.answer: Newborns do not need to be bathed every day. To protect the skin's natural oils, bathing 2-3 times a week is sufficient. Daily, you can wipe their face, hands, and diaper area with a damp, soft cloth. As the baby grows and becomes more active, you can increase the frequency of bathing.
faq.question: How often should you bathe a baby?

faq.answer: The ideal water temperature for a baby bath is approximately 37°C. This is very close to normal body temperature. The most reliable way to check the water temperature is to use a bath thermometer. If you don't have a thermometer, immerse the inside of your elbow or wrist in the water; the water should feel pleasantly warm, not hot.
faq.question: What should be the water temperature when bathing a baby?

faq.answer: It is recommended not to fully immerse the baby in water until the umbilical cord has fallen off and healed completely. During this period, it is important to keep the umbilical cord as dry as possible to reduce the risk of infection. Instead, you can clean the baby's body in sections with a soft sponge or cloth dipped in warm water (sponge bath). Follow your doctor's specific instructions.
faq.question: Can a baby be fully bathed if the umbilical cord has not fallen off?

faq.answer: The most important and golden rule is never to leave the baby alone in the bath, not even for a second. A baby can drown in just a few centimeters of water. Before starting the bath, prepare all supplies such as towels, diapers, and clothes within reach so you don't have to leave the baby's side during the process. Always support the baby with one hand.

articles.title: Newborn Jaundice: A Parent's Guide
articles.excerpt: Newborn jaundice is a common condition that always requires medical evaluation. Learn about its causes, dangerous signs, and proper care guidelines.
articles.content:
You've brought your baby home, but after a few days, you notice a yellowish discoloration on their skin or the whites of their eyes. This sight naturally worries many new parents. This condition is called newborn jaundice and is quite common in babies.

While newborn jaundice is often temporary and harmless, it should never be ignored. Every case of jaundice absolutely requires medical evaluation and measurement of bilirubin levels. It is impossible and potentially dangerous to determine the severity of jaundice based solely on skin color, its spread, or the number of wet diapers. Let's explore in detail why this process occurs, in which cases medical intervention is crucial, and how you can support your baby during this period.

Why Does Jaundice Occur? The Role of Bilirubin

While in the womb, babies need more red blood cells (erythrocytes) to efficiently carry oxygen. After birth, as the baby's lungs begin to function, these extra cells are no longer needed and naturally start to break down. During this breakdown process, a yellow pigment called bilirubin is produced.

An adult's liver easily processes this bilirubin and excretes it from the body. However, a newborn baby's liver is not yet fully mature and cannot perform this process at the same speed. As a result, the accumulated bilirubin in the blood causes the skin, mucous membranes, and eyeballs to turn yellow. The speed of this process and the level of bilirubin in the blood are key factors that determine the type of jaundice and whether treatment is needed.

Types of Jaundice: Physiological and Pathological Jaundice

The vast majority of jaundice seen in newborns is called physiological jaundice. This is part of the baby's adaptation process to new life. The main characteristics of physiological jaundice are:

  • It usually begins 24 hours after birth, i.e., on the 2nd or 3rd day.
  • Bilirubin levels typically peak around the 4th-5th day.
  • As the baby's liver begins to work more efficiently and they feed regularly, it gradually subsides, usually within 1-2 weeks.

However, in some cases, jaundice can be a sign of a more serious health problem. This is called pathological jaundice and requires urgent medical intervention. Some signs of pathological jaundice include:

  • Early onset: Appearing within the first 24 hours after birth.
  • High levels: Bilirubin levels rising very rapidly and to dangerous levels.
  • Prolonged duration: Lasting longer than 14 days in full-term babies and longer than 21 days in premature babies (prolonged jaundice).
  • Other causes: Blood group incompatibility (Rh or ABO incompatibility between mother and baby), infections, liver problems, or certain genetic diseases can cause pathological jaundice.

Jaundice can worsen in babies who do not receive enough milk. In such cases, an effective feeding plan is crucial, but feeding does not replace bilirubin testing and necessary phototherapy. The cause of prolonged jaundice may not always be dangerous; if it persists after 14 days in full-term babies or 21 days in premature babies, it should be evaluated by a doctor.

Danger Signs: When to Seek Immediate Medical Attention?

If you notice any signs of jaundice in your newborn, it is important to inform your pediatrician or the birthing medical staff that same day to assess the situation. The following situations require urgent medical attention, and you should contact a doctor immediately:

  • Jaundice started within the first 24 hours after birth. This always requires urgent evaluation.
  • The yellowing is increasing, the skin color is becoming darker yellow or orange, especially spreading to the arms and legs.
  • The baby is very lethargic and sleepy, difficult to wake, or does not wake to feed.
  • The baby refuses to feed or sucks weakly.
  • The baby's body temperature is 38°C or higher, or conversely, the body is very cold (below 36°C).
  • The baby has difficulty breathing or pauses in breathing.
  • The baby's muscle tone is abnormal (very floppy or, conversely, arching their body and neck unusually backward).
  • Stools are very light-colored (chalky white) or urine is dark tea-colored (this can be a sign of a liver problem and it is important to contact a doctor the same day).
  • The baby's urine output has decreased (fewer than 5 wet diapers per day after day 6).

The doctor will perform a test to measure bilirubin levels, either with a special device on the skin or with a blood test. The necessity of treatment is determined based on the baby's age (in hours), gestational week, weight, and other risk factors. The main treatment method is phototherapy (light therapy). In very rare and severe cases, a blood transfusion may be required.

Support at Home: Proper Feeding and Monitoring

Once a serious condition has been ruled out by a doctor, the most effective way to manage physiological jaundice is to ensure the baby feeds frequently and adequately. Feeding increases bowel activity and helps excrete bilirubin through stool.

  • Frequent feeding: Try to feed your baby every 2-3 hours, meaning typically 8-12 times within 24 hours. If the baby is sleepy, gently wake them to feed.
  • Effective feeding: Ensure the baby latches correctly to the breast and sucks actively. This will ensure they receive enough milk. If needed, seek support from a lactation consultant.
  • DO NOT give water or sugar water: Never give your baby water, sugar water, or other liquids without a doctor's prescription. This can fill their stomach, interfere with breastfeeding, reduce their feeding, and disrupt electrolyte balance.
  • Do not treat with sunlight: Placing the baby in direct sunlight or by a window is not a safe substitute for medical phototherapy. The light dosage is uncontrolled and can cause burns, overheating, and dehydration. Necessary phototherapy is performed under medical supervision with specialized equipment.

Before discharge from the hospital, your doctor should assess the risk of jaundice and schedule a follow-up appointment for a few days later. Be sure to attend this appointment.

Importance of Monitoring Feeding and Diaper Count

Diaper count provides additional information about feeding and fluid intake but does not indicate bilirubin levels or that jaundice is safe. The number of wet diapers gradually increases in the first few days; from day 5 onwards, at least 6 well-soaked diapers in 24 hours is a useful guide. Stool frequency varies depending on the type of feeding and age. Follow your doctor's test and re-examination plan.

Baby's Age Number of Wet Diapers (minimum)
Day 1 1+
Day 2 2+
Day 3 3+
Day 4 4+
Day 5 and onwards 6+

Remember that this table is only a guide and cannot be used to diagnose your baby's condition. If your baby's diaper count is less than these indicators or if you have any concerns about jaundice, be sure to consult your doctor.

Keep Related Notes in One Place with Anacan

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Feeding records: Record the side and duration of breastfeeding with a timer, and the volume of formula in ml. Duration does not measure the volume of milk consumed; discuss the records in conjunction with the baby's weight and clinical evaluation.
  • Diaper records: Record the time of wet, soiled, and mixed diapers. This information can help the doctor assess feeding, but it does not independently diagnose dehydration or other illnesses.
  • Doctor's appointments: Schedule doctor's appointments and vaccination dates in the calendar. Do not wait for the next appointment date if there are urgent signs.
  • Growth charts: Enter weight, height, and head circumference measurements with the appropriate date and discuss growth dynamics with your pediatrician.

Feeding, sleep, and diaper records can be shared in the Doctor's Report. Available access and Premium terms for tools apply. In case of urgent signs, do not delay medical help to write a note in the app.

faq.answer: Newborn jaundice is when a baby's skin and eyes turn yellow. This happens due to an increase in a substance called bilirubin in the blood. Bilirubin is produced when red blood cells break down and is normally removed from the body by the liver. Since newborns' livers are not yet fully mature, this process can be slow, leading to jaundice.
faq.question: What is newborn jaundice and why does it occur?

faq.answer: Feed your breastfed newborn typically 24 times in 8-12 hours, according to hunger cues and your doctor's plan. Formula volume and frequency are individually chosen. For a very sleepy baby who is difficult to wake, do not just try again; seek immediate medical help. Feeding does not replace necessary phototherapy.
faq.question: How should I feed my baby during jaundice?

faq.answer: Contact your pediatrician or birthing staff the same day you notice new jaundice. Jaundice starting within the first 24 hours must be evaluated immediately. Difficulty waking, poor feeding, a fever of 38°C or higher, or breathing problems are urgent. White stools and dark urine, or jaundice lasting longer than 14 days in full-term babies or 21 days in premature babies, should also be evaluated.
faq.question: When should I contact a doctor for jaundice?

faq.answer: No. Direct sunlight and window light are not safe substitutes for specialized medical phototherapy. The light dosage is uncontrolled, and the baby can get burned or overheat, leading to dehydration. Follow your doctor's instructions regarding bilirubin testing, feeding plan, and phototherapy if needed.

articles.title: Supporting Your Baby's Head and Neck: A Safety Guide for the First Months
articles.excerpt: Properly supporting a newborn's head and neck is crucial for their health. Safe holding techniques and tips for strengthening neck muscles.
articles.content:
When you hold a newborn for the first time, you immediately feel how delicate they are and how much their head needs support. The sudden tilting of a baby's head backward or sideways worries many new parents. This concern is completely natural and stems from the baby's anatomical characteristics.

In the first months of life, babies do not have strong enough neck muscles to independently hold and control their heads. For this reason, you must always support your baby's head and neck when you pick them up, carry them, or change their position. Most babies achieve reliable head control by about 4 months of age, but every baby's developmental pace is different. For premature babies, reaching this milestone may take longer according to their adjusted age.

Why is Head Support Vital in the First Months?

A newborn's body structure differs significantly from that of an adult. These differences explain the importance of head and neck support:

  • Proportionally Large Head: A newborn's head is quite large and heavy relative to the rest of their body. This makes it difficult for their weak neck muscles to support this weight.
  • Underdeveloped Neck Muscles: The baby's neck muscles and ligaments are not yet fully formed and strengthened. For this reason, without support, the head can easily and suddenly fall backward, forward, or sideways. While a slight tremor of the head is normal, it is important to protect against sudden and sharp movements.
  • Keeping the Airway Clear: If the baby's head tilts too far forward and their chin is pressed against their chest, their narrow and soft airways can become constricted, obstructing airflow. This makes breathing difficult. When holding a baby in your arms or in a carrier, always ensure their face is visible and there is at least a two-finger gap between their chin and chest.
  • Shaking Hazard: Never shake a baby, neither out of anger nor for play. Rapid back-and-forth movement of the head without support can lead to "Shaken Baby Syndrome," which can cause serious brain and spinal injuries.

Safe Ways to Pick Up and Hold Your Baby

When lifting your baby from the crib, carrying them in your arms, or during daily care, follow these simple but vital steps:

  • When Lifting from the Crib: Place one hand, palm open, under the baby's head and neck. With your other hand, support their hips and back. Lift their body as a whole, gently and simultaneously.
  • “Cradle Hold”: When holding the baby horizontally in your arms, place their head in the crook of your arm. This position supports their head, neck, and spine in alignment. You can use your other hand to support their hips or body.
  • When Holding Over the Shoulder: Hold the baby vertically with their chin resting on your shoulder. With one hand, always support the back of their head and neck, and with the other hand, hold their back and hips.
  • Support During Care: When changing clothes or bathing, even when laying the baby down, always provide gentle support to the neck area with one hand to prevent their head from suddenly falling backward.
  • Baby Carriers and Slings: When using a carrier or sling, ensure the baby's head and neck are fully supported, their face is visible, and their airway is clear. The baby's body should not be curled in the carrier, and their chin should not be pressed against their chest.

Exercise to Strengthen Neck Muscles: “Tummy Time”

The most effective and important activity for the development of a baby's neck, shoulder, and back muscles and for learning to hold their head independently is called “Tummy Time.”

When and How to Start Tummy Time?

You can start tummy time immediately after coming home from the hospital, without waiting for the umbilical cord to fall off. Initially, start with several sessions a day, each lasting only 1-2 minutes, when the baby is awake and comfortable. As the baby gets used to it and strengthens, you can gradually increase this duration. You can do this exercise on a clean blanket on the floor or even lying on your own chest.

Expectations by Developmental Stages

The table below shows the typical development of a baby during tummy time, but remember that every baby develops at an individual pace.

Age (Approximate) Expected Skills
Newborn When on their tummy, places their cheek on the ground, can briefly turn their head from one side to the other.
1-2 Months Starts to lift their head off the ground for short periods, can even hold it for a few seconds.
3 Months Lifts head and chest higher by leaning on elbows, holds head more steadily.
4 Months Holds head upright and steady, easily turns head right and left to observe surroundings.

Important Warning: Tummy time exercises should only be performed when the baby is fully awake and under continuous supervision of an adult. Never let a baby sleep on their tummy, as this increases the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS).

When to Consult a Pediatrician?

While every baby's development is different, some signs require medical advice:

  • If they have difficulty holding their head unsupported despite being 4 months old: If the baby's head is still very “floppy” and constantly falls backward or sideways.
  • Asymmetry: If they constantly tilt their head to only one side or have difficulty turning their head to the other side (this could be a sign of torticollis).
  • Abnormal Muscle Tone: If their body feels excessively stiff and tense or, conversely, very soft and “floppy” when you pick them up.
  • Developmental Regression: If they lose a skill they previously acquired (e.g., lifting their head).
  • Situations Requiring Emergency Medical Attention: If you observe difficulty breathing, blueness of the skin or lips (cyanosis), call emergency services immediately. For babies younger than 3 months, a fever of 38°C or higher also requires urgent medical evaluation.

Keep Anacan-Related Notes in One Place

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Growth charts: Enter weight, height, and head circumference measurements with the appropriate date and discuss growth dynamics with your pediatrician.
  • Sleep history: Track daily rhythm by recording sleep start and end times with a timer. The app does not monitor breathing during sleep and does not replace safe sleep guidelines.

Feeding, sleep, and diaper records can be shared in the Doctor's Report. Available access and Premium terms for tools apply. Do not delay medical assistance to write a note in the app for urgent symptoms.

At this age, most babies have strengthened their neck muscles sufficiently to hold their heads independently. However, every baby is different, and for premature babies, this period may be longer according to their adjusted age.
faq.question: How long should a baby's head be supported?

faq.answer: “Tummy Time” is when a baby is placed on their tummy while awake and supervised. This strengthens the neck, shoulder, and back muscles. You can start immediately after coming home from the hospital, with several 1-2 minute sessions a day. Never let a baby sleep on their tummy.
faq.question: What is “Tummy Time” and when can it be started?

faq.answer: Leaving the head unsupported can cause it to suddenly fall backward or sideways. This can lead to strained neck muscles and discomfort. The most serious risk is when the head tilts forward, pressing the chin against the chest and obstructing the airway. Shaking a baby is very dangerous and can cause serious brain injuries.
faq.question: What risks can result from not supporting a baby's head?

faq.answer: Consult a pediatrician if your baby cannot hold their head unsupported despite being 4 months old, constantly tilts their head to only one side, or their body appears excessively tense or floppy. Difficulty breathing, blueness of the skin, or a fever above 38°C in a baby younger than 3 months requires urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Baby's Safe Sleep Environment: Crib Selection and Proper Use Guidelines
articles.excerpt: Choosing and using a crib is critical for your baby's safe and healthy sleep. Create the ideal sleep environment for your baby with this guide.
articles.content:
Newborn babies spend a large part of the day, approximately 16-18 hours, sleeping. This means your baby will spend most of their time in their crib during the first months of life. Parents usually focus on the design, color, and compatibility with the room's decor when choosing a crib. However, the golden rule never changes: the baby's crib must be comfortable, and most importantly, absolutely safe.

Creating a healthy and safe sleep environment is the most crucial step for both your baby's healthy development and your peace of mind at night. This is the most effective way to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and other sleep-related accidents. Let's take a detailed look at what an ideal crib environment should be like.

Crib Selection: Compliance with Standards and Structure

When choosing a crib, it is vital to prioritize its compliance with safety standards over aesthetic appearance. When buying a new crib, ensure it meets current safety standards. If you are using a second-hand crib, check that it has no damaged, worn, or broken parts.

The crib must have a sturdy construction, with no sharp edges or protrusions. The distance between the bars on the sides of the crib should not exceed 6 cm, to prevent the baby's head from passing through or their body from getting trapped. Also, ensure that the paints used on the crib are non-toxic, water-based, and made from materials safe for babies. It is recommended that your baby sleeps in the same room as you, but in their own separate crib, for at least the first 6 months, and ideally for 1 year. This makes night feedings easier and significantly reduces the risk of SIDS.

Mattress Selection: Firm, Flat, and Snug Fit

We adults may love sleeping on cloud-soft beds, but this rule absolutely does not apply to babies. A baby's mattress must be firm and completely flat. Soft mattresses, memory foam, or any additional soft toppers can indent around the baby's nose and mouth when they turn face down, obstructing their breathing and sharply increasing the risk of suffocation. Even for babies with reflux, it is not recommended to incline the crib or mattress.

The mattress should fit snugly within the crib frame. There should be no more than two fingers' width of space between the mattress and the crib sides. If there is a gap, it poses a danger of the baby's head, hand, or foot getting trapped in that space. Only a tightly fitted sheet, fully secured to the mattress, should be used on the mattress. There should be no other under or over coverings.

"Empty Crib – Safe Crib" Rule

Beautiful pillows, large plush toys, and thick blankets may look very appealing in social media photos. However, in reality, they have no place in a baby's crib. The inside of the crib must be completely empty. This is the most important step to minimize the risk of suffocation and SIDS.

  • Absolutely no pillows: Babies up to 1 year of age do not need pillows. Pillows pose a serious suffocation hazard.
  • No loose and heavy coverings: There should be no soft toys, blankets, quilts, bumper pads, baby nests, or pillow-like positioners inside the crib. These items can cover the baby's face or restrict their movement, making breathing difficult.
  • Do not use weighted products: Weighted swaddles, sleep sacks, and blankets are not suitable for baby sleep. A home monitor also does not replace safe sleep guidelines.
  • Safe alternative: If you are concerned about your baby getting cold, instead of covering them with a thick blanket, dress them in a season-appropriate, sleeveless or long-sleeved sleep sack. This keeps the baby warm but does not pose a risk of covering their face.
  • Mobile toys: Mobile toys hung above the crib should be removed immediately when the baby attempts to push up on their hands and knees (usually around 4-5 months) or when they reach the age limit recommended by the manufacturer, to prevent them from pulling them down and harming themselves.

Safe Sleep Position and Swaddling Rules

The most important detail complementing a safe crib environment is the baby's sleeping position. For every sleep – whether night or day – you must always place the baby on their back. Sleeping on their stomach or side significantly increases the risk of SIDS. Some babies may not like sleeping on their back, but adhering to this rule is essential for safety.

Once the baby learns to roll freely from tummy to back and back to tummy, if they roll onto their stomach in their sleep, there is no need to turn them back. At this stage, their neck muscles are strong enough to turn their head. However, you should always place them on their back when putting them in the crib.

Swaddling can soothe a baby, but it is important to do it safely. Swaddle only before the baby starts attempting to roll. As soon as you see the first signs of rolling (attempting to turn to the side), you must stop swaddling immediately. A swaddled baby who rolls onto their stomach has difficulty turning back because their arms are not free, creating a risk of suffocation.

Crib Placement in the Room and Environment

The crib's position in the room is as important as its structure. Proper placement ensures the baby's comfort and safety.

  • Keep the crib away from direct sunlight, heat radiators, air conditioner drafts, or other heating/cooling sources. The room temperature should be comfortable for adults. Avoid over-dressing the baby or overheating the room. You can check their temperature by touching the back of their neck; if they are sweaty, it means it's too hot.
  • Choose a spot away from windows and especially from curtain or blind cords. These cords are a serious suffocation hazard for babies.
  • Place the crib at a safe distance from walls or other furniture to prevent the baby from getting trapped between them as they grow.
  • Do not smoke in the baby's bedroom or at home. Secondhand smoke is one of the main factors increasing the risk of SIDS.

When to Contact a Doctor?

If you have concerns about your baby's sleep habits, do not hesitate to talk to your doctor or nurse. It is especially important to seek medical attention in the following cases:

  • If the baby experiences difficulty breathing during sleep (pauses in breathing, wheezing, rapid or labored breathing).
  • If a baby younger than 3 months has a rectal temperature of 38°C or higher, this may be a situation requiring urgent medical attention. Contact a doctor immediately.
  • If the baby's skin, lips, or nails turn blue or pale.
  • If it is harder than usual to wake the baby or if they are excessively lethargic.

Remember, an app or tracker alone cannot diagnose. Trust your parental instincts and seek professional advice in any situation you suspect.

articles.title: Breast Pump: Protecting Lactation and Supporting Milk Production
articles.excerpt: Breast pumps are invaluable helpers on the motherhood journey. This tool helps protect lactation, stimulate milk production, and provide comfort to the mother.
articles.content:
Breastfeeding doesn't always proceed with the ideal scenario of simply nursing the baby directly from the breast. There are stages in the motherhood journey when, for various reasons, it's not possible to breastfeed the baby at that moment. Sometimes, the necessity to return to work, sometimes the baby's inability to latch properly, and sometimes simply the mother's need for a few hours of uninterrupted sleep bring breast pumps into play.

Breast pumps are not just a means of "extraction"; they are, in fact, an invaluable helper that protects and stimulates the lactation process and grants the mother great freedom. By using this tool correctly, you can both protect your milk supply and ensure your baby always receives breast milk. Let's delve into all the details of this important process, the secrets of choosing a pump, and how to express milk effectively.

Why Might a Breast Pump Be Necessary?

Many mothers think during pregnancy, "I'm at home anyway, why do I need to pump milk?" However, experience shows that having a breast pump is vital in many situations:

  • Reducing Breast Engorgement and Discomfort: In the first days after birth, a sudden and massive influx of milk into the breasts can occur. When breasts become overly engorged or hard, it can be difficult for the baby to latch properly. Pumping a small amount of milk (without fully emptying the breast) at this time softens the breasts, helps the baby nurse comfortably, and increases the mother's comfort.
  • Premature or Special Needs Babies: Babies born prematurely or those in an incubator may not yet have a fully developed suckling reflex. Some babies cannot be fed directly from the breast for medical reasons. In such cases, the mother regularly expressing her milk to feed the baby is the best source of nutrition for their development.
  • Creating a "Milk Bank" for the Future: When the mother has work outside the home, needs to take medication due to illness (after consulting a doctor), or simply wants the baby to spend a few hours with their father, a pre-stored supply of frozen milk prevents the baby from being deprived of breast milk. This provides flexibility and comfort to the mother.
  • Stimulating Milk Production: Sometimes, the mother's milk production does not fully meet the baby's needs. Regular use of a breast pump, especially in the first weeks after birth, sends a signal to the breasts to produce more milk.

Types of Breast Pumps: Which One to Choose?

When buying a pump, your needs, budget, and frequency of use play a key role:

  • Manual Pumps: Suitable for mothers who will pump very rarely (once or 1-2 times a week) or who only want to express a small amount of milk to soften their breasts. They are quiet and do not require electricity, but they can tire the hand and the process can take a long time. Learning manual expression techniques is also very beneficial.
  • Electric Single Pumps: Practical for those who pump 1-2 times a day. They are fast and convenient, but since they only pump one breast at a time, they take longer.
  • Electric Double Pumps: The best choice for working mothers or those who exclusively pump. Pumping both breasts simultaneously saves time and can stimulate prolactin levels in the body more than single pumping, which helps support milk production.

Golden Rules for Effective and Comfortable Pumping

The amount expressed can vary depending on the day, the last feeding, the pump's fit, and your comfort. This amount alone does not indicate whether your milk supply is sufficient or how much the baby drinks from the breast. If the output is low, first check the flange, vacuum, and technique; if there are concerns about weight and wet diapers, seek a professional feeding assessment.

  • Comfortable Start: Sit comfortably and start with a low, pain-free vacuum. A short warm shower can provide comfort to some mothers, but avoid long hot compresses and strong deep massages. Do not forcefully try to "fully empty" a red, hot, and inflamed breast; excessive pumping can worsen engorgement and inflammation.
  • Your Baby's Scent and Picture: Oxytocin, the hormone that facilitates milk flow, is linked to feelings of love and comfort. While pumping, look at pictures of your baby, watch a video of them, or smell a piece of their clothing. Stress blocks oxytocin, while relaxation releases it.
  • Correct Flange Size: The most common mistake! The plastic flange of the breast pump that sits on the nipple must be the correct size. During pumping, the nipple should move freely in the flange tunnel, without rubbing against the walls. At the same time, a large part of the areola should not be pulled into the tunnel. The wrong size causes pain and hinders milk flow.
  • Relaxing Environment and Deep Breathing: Create a comfortable environment during pumping. Sit in a quiet room, take deep breaths, and try to relax.
  • Vacuum Level: Increase the pump's vacuum level to the highest comfortable level that provides effective pumping without causing pain. A high vacuum does not always mean more milk; on the contrary, it can damage the breasts.

Pumping Regimen to Support Milk Production

Mammary glands work on a "supply and demand" principle. The more frequently the breast is emptied, the more the brain receives the signal "more milk is needed." If you think your milk supply is decreasing, it's best to talk to a lactation consultant. Some mothers benefit from the following methods:

Regular Pumping Schedule

If you are separated from your baby for a long time or are exclusively pumping, it is important to establish a regular schedule to maintain milk production. In such cases, you may need to pump every 2-3 hours, meaning approximately 8-12 times a day. Every mother's needs are different, so it's important to find a regimen that suits your body and your baby's needs.

"Power Pumping" Technique (Optional)

This technique is used to mimic the frequent nursing during a baby's growth spurt to increase milk supply. It is not necessary for everyone, and its effectiveness can be individual. You can try applying the following schedule once a day, for one hour:

  1. Pump for 20 minutes.
  2. Take a 10 minute break.
  3. Pump again for 10 minutes.
  4. Another 10 minute break.
  5. Final pump for 10 minutes.

It is recommended to consult a lactation specialist before trying this method.

Safe Storage Guidelines for Breast Milk

To avoid wasting your precious expressed milk, you need to know its exact storage times. These guidelines are for healthy, full-term babies. For babies in the hospital, premature, or with weakened immune systems, learn different storage guidelines from medical personnel.

Environment Temperature Storage Duration
Room temperature Up to 25°C Up to 4 hours
Refrigerator 4°C or lower Up to 4 days
Freezer -18°C or lower Using within 6 months is a conservative choice; for longer storage, refer to freezer conditions and pediatrician's instructions.

Key Rules:

  • Thawing: Thaw frozen milk by placing it in the refrigerator overnight or under cool running water, not at room temperature. Once fully thawed, milk should be used within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator (this period begins after the milk is fully thawed).
  • Warmed milk: After warming or bringing to room temperature, use the milk within 2 hours. Durations may vary across different sources; the stricter medical guideline given for your baby is preferred.
  • Heating: Warm milk in a container of warm water. Never heat in a microwave, as this can reduce the nutritional value of the milk and cause uneven heating, potentially burning the baby's mouth.
  • Re-use: Any milk remaining in the bottle after the baby's feeding should be used or discarded within 2 hours. Never refreeze thawed milk.
  • Cleanliness: After each use, breast pump parts should be washed with warm soapy water and thoroughly air-dried. If the baby is younger than 2 months, premature, or has a weakened immune system, pump parts should be sterilized at least once a day.

When is Professional Help Needed?

Some lactation-related situations may require professional medical attention:

  • Symptoms of Mastitis: If you experience severe pain, redness, swelling in your breasts along with flu-like symptoms (malaise, chills), or have a fever of 38°C or higher, this could be a sign of mastitis. Seek medical attention immediately.
  • Problems with Baby's Weight Gain: If your baby is not gaining enough weight or has fewer wet diapers (less than 6 per day), this may indicate insufficient milk supply or transfer to the baby. Consult a lactation specialist or pediatrician.
  • Persistent Pain or Cracked Nipples: If you experience persistent pain during breastfeeding or pumping, or have unhealing cracked nipples, this may be due to incorrect technique. A lactation specialist can help.
  • Emergency Situation with Baby: A fever of 3°C or higher in babies younger than 38 months requires immediate medical evaluation.

Keep Anacan-Related Notes in One Place

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Feeding records: Record the side and duration of breastfeeding with a timer, and the volume of formula in ml. Duration does not measure the volume of milk consumed; discuss records in conjunction with the baby's weight and clinical assessment.
  • Growth charts: Enter weight, height, and head circumference measurements with the appropriate date and discuss growth dynamics with your pediatrician.

Feeding, sleep, and diaper records can be shared in the Doctor's Report. Available access and Premium terms of the tools apply. Do not delay medical assistance to write a note in the app for emergency symptoms.

If you are just pumping for a stash or pumping at work, your schedule will be different. There is no one-size-fits-all rule.
faq.question: How often should I use a breast pump?

faq.answer: Never warm expressed breast milk in a microwave. The safest method is to slowly warm the milk bottle or bag by placing it in a container of warm water or holding it under warm running water. Check the milk's temperature by dripping a small amount on your wrist – it should be body temperature or slightly warm, not hot.
faq.question: How should I warm expressed breast milk?

faq.answer: After each use, wash all parts of the pump that come into contact with milk with warm, soapy water and allow them to air dry. Sterilization is not required daily, but it is recommended to sterilize these parts at least once a day if your baby is younger than 2 months, premature, or has a weakened immune system.
faq.question: How often should I sterilize breast pump parts?

faq.answer: Not necessarily. Pumping output can vary with pump fit, technique, timing, and comfort, and does not solely measure overall milk supply. The baby's weight, wet diapers, and effective nursing should be assessed. Use a pain-free vacuum and appropriate flange; if you have concerns, consult a lactation specialist.

articles.title: Baby Diaper Choice: The Importance of Comfort, Breathability, and Correct Size
articles.excerpt: Choosing the most suitable diaper for your baby's sensitive skin is crucial for ensuring their comfort and health. Softness, breathability, and the correct size are key criteria.
articles.content:
One of the main products that continuously touches your baby's body in the first years of life is the diaper. This product, in contact with the skin day and night, is not just a means to contain urine and feces; it acts as a "second skin" that directly determines your baby's comfort, sleep quality, and most importantly, skin health. Choosing the right diaper plays a crucial role in preventing problems such as diaper rash, redness, and discomfort.

Choosing among dozens of different brands and varieties on store shelves can be confusing. However, the process becomes easier when you understand the basic principles. There are three main criteria that parents should pay attention to: softness, breathability, and proper fit. These factors help create optimal conditions for your baby's healthy development, considering their sensitive skin. Remember that the most expensive diaper may not always be the best; the main thing is to find one that suits your baby's individual needs.

Softness and Material: Protecting Sensitive Skin

Baby skin is more sensitive and vulnerable to external influences than adult skin. The texture of the inner and outer surface of the diaper is therefore of great importance. Diapers made of harsh material can rub against the inner thighs and abdominal area with every movement of the baby, causing redness and discomfort. Soft materials reduce friction and protect the baby's skin.

Choose a diaper that is soft, absorbent, appropriately sized, and tolerated by your baby's skin. Fragrance can be irritating, but "natural," "hypoallergenic," or expensive does not guarantee superiority. Disposable and properly cared-for cloth diapers can be suitable. Fold the top edge of the diaper below the navel to avoid rubbing against the umbilical stump. For a new brand, first try a small pack.

Breathability: The Strongest Defense Against Diaper Rash

Diaper rash primarily arises from a combination of three factors: moisture, heat, and friction. The breathability of the diaper helps minimize the impact of these factors. Diapers without airflow create a "greenhouse effect" inside. Ammonia from urine and feces can very quickly damage the skin barrier in this closed and warm environment.

Most modern diapers have a micro-porous outer layer that retains liquid inside but allows air and vapor to escape. This helps keep the baby's bottom drier and protects skin health. The wetness indicator (usually a color-changing strip) found in some diapers can be a useful aid, but this should not be an excuse to delay changing the diaper for a long time. The main thing is to regularly check the diaper's fullness and ensure the baby's comfort.

Correct Size and Fit: Preventing Leaks

Even the highest quality diaper will not be effective if it is not chosen in the correct size and does not fit the body perfectly. One of the main causes of leaks is choosing the wrong size. The weight ranges on diapers (e.g., 4-8 kg) are merely a guide. A tall and slender baby and a short and chubby baby of the same weight may require different sizes or brands.

  • Signs of a small diaper: If the diaper leaves red marks on your baby's waist or thighs when removed, if the tabs are difficult to fasten, or if leaks occur frequently, it's time to move up a size.
  • Signs of a large diaper: If there are large gaps around the waist of the diaper, if the leg openings are loose, and if the diaper slides down when the baby moves, the diaper is too large.

After fastening the diaper, you should be able to comfortably place two fingers between the waist of the diaper and your baby's tummy. This indicates that the diaper is neither too tight nor too loose. Also, make sure that the protective ruffles around the legs are always pulled outwards. Ruffles tucked inside can cause leaks.

Diaper Changing and Skin Care Routine

Even the best diaper loses its function if not changed in time. Regular diaper changes are essential to protect your baby's skin health.

The baby's diaper should be changed as soon as it is wet or immediately after a bowel movement. For newborns, this can be up to 10-12 times a day, and for older babies, 6-8 times a day. If the baby has had a bowel movement during sleep or the diaper is excessively full, it must be changed without waiting to avoid disturbing their sleep.

When changing the diaper, clean your baby's bottom with lukewarm water and cotton, or with fragrance-free, hypoallergenic wet wipes. For girls, always clean from front to back to reduce the risk of infection. Allow the skin to dry completely. Applying a protective diaper rash cream with each diaper change can create a barrier that protects the skin from moisture.

Safety is paramount: Never leave your baby unattended, even for a second, on a high surface like a changing table. Keep all supplies ready and within reach.

When to Consult a Doctor?

Mild redness and diaper rash usually clear up within a few days with proper home care. However, in some cases, it is important to consult a doctor:

  • If the redness does not improve after 2-3 days or worsens.
  • If bright red spots, open sores, blisters, or pus-filled pimples appear on the skin (this may be a sign of a fungal or bacterial infection).
  • If the baby has a fever (especially in babies younger than 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or higher requires urgent medical attention).
  • If the baby is very uncomfortable, cries from pain during diaper changes, or refuses to feed.
  • If the rash spreads beyond the diaper area.

Keep Related Notes in One Place with Anacan

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Diaper logs: Record the time of wet, soiled, and mixed diapers. This information can help the doctor assess feeding, but it does not diagnose dehydration or other illnesses on its own.
  • Growth charts: Enter weight, height, and head circumference measurements with the appropriate date and discuss growth dynamics with your pediatrician.

Feeding, sleep, and diaper records can be shared in the Doctor's Report. Available access and Premium terms for tools apply. Do not delay medical assistance to write a note in the application in case of an emergency.

articles.title: Baby Diaper Changing: Skin Health and Rash Prevention
articles.excerpt: Diaper changing frequency and proper techniques play a crucial role in protecting a baby's sensitive skin and preventing diaper rashes.
articles.content:
One of the most fundamental and daily routines in baby care is, undoubtedly, changing diapers. Although it may seem like a simple household chore at first glance, changing diapers on time and correctly is vital for your baby's health. The frequency of diaper changes and hygiene rules play a significant role in protecting your baby's sensitive skin and preventing unpleasant redness, i.e., diaper rash.

In this article, we will explain in detail why baby skin is so sensitive, how diaper rash develops, and what steps you need to take to protect against it. We will also look at how the Anacan app can simplify this daily routine. Remember, your baby's comfort and health are in your hands.

Why is Baby Skin So Sensitive?

Newborn babies' skin is thinner, more sensitive, and more defenseless against external influences compared to adult skin. Their skin's protective barrier has not yet fully developed, which makes it more susceptible to infections and irritation. When these skin characteristics are combined with moisture and warmth in the diaper area, they create ideal conditions for the development of diaper rash.

  • Weak Protective Barrier:Since the skin's natural protective barrier is not yet fully formed, it has difficulty retaining moisture and protecting itself from external irritants.
  • High Humidity:The diaper area remains constantly moist and warm, creating a favorable environment for the proliferation of bacteria and fungi.
  • pH Balance:The pH level of baby skin is different from adults' and can easily change under the influence of urine and feces, which weakens the skin's protective function.
  • Friction:The rubbing of the diaper against the skin, especially in active babies, can cause mechanical irritation.

How Does Diaper Rash (Dermatitis) Develop?

Diaper rash, medically known as diaper dermatitis, is one of the most common skin problems in babies. This condition is characterized by redness, irritation, and sometimes pain in the diaper area. The main causes of diaper rash are:

  • Prolonged Contact:When ammonia in urine and enzymes in feces remain in contact with the skin for a long time, they damage the skin's natural protective barrier and cause irritation.
  • Moist Environment:The moist and warm environment inside the diaper creates ideal conditions for the rapid proliferation of bacteria and fungi (especially Candida). These microorganisms cause inflammation of the skin.
  • Dietary Changes:Changes in a baby's diet (e.g., transitioning to solid foods, introducing new foods) can alter stool composition, which may lead to diaper rash. Antibiotic use can also disrupt gut flora, paving the way for rashes.
  • Sensitive Skin and Chemical Irritants:Some babies have more sensitive skin than others. Additionally, fragrances and chemicals in certain diapers or wet wipes can cause irritation.

Golden Rules for Diaper Changing

To keep your baby's skin dry, healthy, and rash-free, it's enough to follow these simple yet crucial rules:

1. Check Frequently and Change Immediately

Check your baby's diaper frequently. A soiled diaper should be changed immediately, and a wet diaper as soon as possible. Leaving a dirty diaper on for a long time is a major risk factor for skin irritation. For newborns, the number of wet diapers indicates adequate feeding: approximately one wet diaper on the first day, two on the second day is normal, and this number should reach at least six per day by the fifth day. Diaper changing frequency varies with the baby's age and feeding. If the baby has had a bowel movement at night, it is important to wake them up and change it immediately. If there is only urine, highly absorbent night diapers can help keep the skin dry, but this requires an individual approach based on each baby's skin sensitivity.

2. Gentle and Thorough Cleaning

When changing a diaper, the best way to clean the skin is to use lukewarm running water or a soft cotton cloth soaked in water. If it is necessary to use wet wipes, choose hypoallergenic ones that are alcohol- and fragrance-free. During cleaning, especially for girls, movements should always be from front to back to prevent infections.

3. Complete Drying and Air Baths

After cleaning, it is very important to dry the skin completely. Instead of rubbing the skin, gently pat it dry with a soft towel. Ensure all skin folds are dry. Giving your baby "air baths" (being diaper-free) for 5-10 minutes during each diaper change or several times a day helps the skin breathe and heal naturally. Remember, never leave your baby unattended on a high surface like a changing table.

4. Correct Use of Barrier Creams

You can use barrier creams to prevent diaper rash or to heal mild redness. Creams containing zinc oxide or petrolatum (Vaseline) create a thin barrier on the skin, protecting it from moisture and irritants. Apply the cream in a thin layer to clean and completely dry skin. Avoid using talcum powder, as its particles can enter the baby's respiratory tract. Also, do not use harsh antiseptic or steroid-containing ointments without medical advice.

When to Consult a Doctor?

Most diaper rashes improve within 2-3 days with proper home care. However, it is important to consult a doctor in the following cases:

  • The rash does not improve within 2-3 days; instead, it worsens or spreads.
  • Bright red spots, blisters, pus-filled pimples, or open sores appear on the skin.
  • Fever is observed in the baby (especially in babies younger than 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or higher requires immediate medical attention).
  • The baby is excessively restless, crying, and experiences pain when the diaper area is touched.
  • If diarrhea or other signs of discomfort accompany the rash.

These symptoms may indicate a more serious problem, such as a fungal or bacterial infection, and may require specific treatment. It is not possible to diagnose with an app or by counting; only a doctor can make an accurate diagnosis.

articles.title: Umbilical Cord Care in Newborns: Healing Process and Proper Care
articles.excerpt: Support the natural healing process of your baby's umbilical cord. Learn about clean and dry care practices, signs of infection, and when to consult a doctor.
articles.content:
In the first days after returning home from the hospital, holding your baby is the greatest happiness in the world. However, that small umbilical cord stump on their tiny body causes anxiety and worry for many new parents. Questions like "Will it hurt if I touch it?", "How should I clean it?", "When will it fall off?" might occupy your mind.

First and foremost, take a deep breath: the drying and falling off of the umbilical cord stump is a natural process. There are no nerve endings in the dried umbilical cord stump, but the surrounding skin is sensitive; redness and pain upon touch can be signs of infection. Your main task is to support this process without interference, simply by keeping the area clean and dry. Remember that every baby is different and the healing time may vary, but the basic principles remain the same.

What is the Umbilical Cord Stump and When Does It Fall Off?

While your baby was in the womb, they received all nutrition and oxygen through the umbilical cord. Immediately after birth, this cord is cut, leaving a small stump behind. This stump no longer performs its function and will gradually dry out and separate from the body.

  • How does the process work? The umbilical cord stump gradually dries, changing color from yellowish-green to dark brown or black. This is a completely normal process and indicates that the cord is drying and separating from the body.
  • How many days does it take? In most babies, the umbilical cord stump falls off completely on its own within 1 to 3 weeks after birth. In some cases, this period may be slightly shorter or longer. However, if it lasts longer than 3 weeks, it is recommended to consult a doctor.

The most important principle during this process is to be patient. Nature does its work, and your task is to protect the area from external irritants and ensure its cleanliness.

Key Rules for Umbilical Cord Care: Keep it Clean and Dry

In modern pediatrics, the main motto for umbilical cord care is the principle of "keep it clean and dry." The daily use of alcohol or other antiseptic solutions, once widely practiced, is no longer recommended, as it can slow down the natural healing process and irritate the skin. However, in some specific cases, under a doctor's instruction, agents like chlorhexidine may be used.

1. Always Keep it Dry and Clean

Allowing the umbilical area to be exposed to air accelerates the drying process. If the umbilical area gets dirty or comes into contact with urine, gently wipe it with a cotton swab moistened with clean water and immediately pat it completely dry with a clean, soft cloth. Moisture can increase the risk of infection, so dryness is very important.

2. Fold the Diaper Below the Umbilicus

Fold the top edge of the baby's diaper down, away from the umbilical cord stump, so it doesn't cover it. This is important for two reasons:

  • It allows the umbilical cord to air out and helps it dry.
  • It prevents the diaper from rubbing against and irritating the umbilical cord, and from absorbing moisture if it comes into contact with urine.

Some newborn diapers have a special cutout for the umbilical cord for this purpose.

3. Pay Attention to Bathing

Until the umbilical cord falls off, sponge bathing (sponge bath) is a safer method than fully immersing the baby in a bathtub. This prevents the umbilical area from getting wet and reduces the risk of infection. If your doctor at discharge has not advised otherwise, prefer this method. After the cord falls off and the area is completely healed, you can comfortably bathe your baby in a tub.

4. Dress in Loose, Breathable Clothing

Dress your baby in loose-fitting clothes made of cotton material that do not constrict their body. Bodysuits or shirts should allow air circulation around the umbilical area. Tight and synthetic clothing can restrict airflow and lead to moisture accumulation, which increases the risk of infection.

What NOT to Do?

You may hear various advice from others, but for your baby's health, avoid these incorrect practices:

  • ❌ Absolutely do not pull or pick: Even if the umbilical cord stump looks like it's "hanging by a thread," it should fall off on its own. Prematurely pulling it off can cause bleeding, infection, or injury to the umbilical area.
  • ❌ Do not use folk remedies: Sticking coins on the umbilical cord, tightly binding it with bandages, or applying oils, herbal infusions, or other ointments sharply increases the risk of infection and can disrupt the healing process.
  • ❌ Do not use antiseptics without a doctor's prescription: Unless your doctor specifically instructs you, there is no need to wipe the umbilical cord daily with alcohol or other agents.

When to Consult a Doctor?

Although umbilical cord healing usually proceeds without problems, it is vital to recognize signs of infection (omphalitis) in time. If you observe any of the following, consult a doctor immediately:

  • Spreading Redness and Swelling: Redness, swelling, or warmth to the touch of the skin around the umbilical cord. If the redness spreads beyond a small spot, this is a condition requiring urgent medical attention.
  • Purulent and Foul-Smelling Discharge: If yellowish-green, foul-smelling fluid (pus) comes from the umbilical cord, this is a clear sign of infection and requires immediate medical examination.
  • Persistent Bleeding: A drop or two of dried blood when the cord falls off is normal. However, if you see active, fresh blood stains in the diaper or if the bleeding does not stop, consult a doctor.
  • High Fever or General Discomfort: If the baby's body temperature is 38°C or higher (especially in babies younger than 3 months), if they are excessively sleepy, refuse to feed, or are very irritable, this could be a sign of a serious infection and requires urgent medical attention.
  • Delayed Falling Off or Granuloma: If the umbilical cord has not fallen off after 3 weeks, consult a doctor. If a moist, pinkish-red, fleshy tissue (umbilical granuloma) remains in the umbilical area after it falls off, show it to a doctor. Do not use salt or other chemicals at home without medical advice.

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's existing tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Diaper records: Record the times of wet, soiled, and mixed diapers. This information can help the doctor assess feeding, but it does not diagnose dehydration or other illnesses on its own.
  • Hospital bag: Use the checklist from the Hospital Bag tool and add items required by your specific hospital.
  • Doctor appointments: Schedule doctor appointments and vaccination dates in the calendar. Do not wait for the next appointment date if there are urgent symptoms.

faq.answer: Until the umbilical cord falls off, it is recommended to sponge bathe the baby (wiping their body with a damp cloth). This helps keep the umbilical area dry and reduces the risk of infection. After the cord falls off and the area is completely healed, you can bathe your baby in a tub.
faq.question: How should I bathe my baby until the umbilical cord falls off?

faq.answer: Most umbilical stumps detach within 1-3 weeks. If it hasn't fallen off after three weeks, consult a pediatrician to assess the cause and do not attempt to remove it yourself. If there is redness, pus, fever, or if the baby appears ill, seek medical attention without delay.
faq.question: What should I do if the umbilical cord has not fallen off after 3 weeks?

faq.answer: Signs of infection include spreading redness and swelling around the navel, foul-smelling yellowish-green discharge (pus), the baby crying when the umbilical area is touched, or a fever above 38°C. If you observe any of these symptoms, consult a doctor immediately, as an umbilical infection can become serious.

articles.title: Newborn Baby Urine: Color Changes and Warning Signs
articles.excerpt: Did you notice orange, pink spots, or dark urine in your baby's diaper? Learn the causes of these conditions, normal urine output, and which signs require a doctor's visit.
articles.content:
Seeing dark yellow, orange, or even pinkish-red spots in your newborn's diaper can naturally worry any parent. The question, “Is this blood?” might cross your mind. While this sight indeed requires attention, it is often a common occurrence in the first few days and is usually related to the baby's body adapting to new life. However, it can also be a signal that the baby is not getting enough fluids.

In this article, we will explain in detail the reasons behind these color changes in the diaper, how long they can be considered normal, and in which cases it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention. Remember, if you have any doubts about your baby's health, the best course of action is always to consult a pediatrician. This information is for general educational purposes only.

Why is Urine Dark and Concentrated in the First Days?

During the first few days after birth, the fluid from the mother's breasts is not “mature milk” but colostrum. Although colostrum is very small in quantity (a few teaspoons per feeding), it is extremely rich in antibodies and nutrients that strengthen the baby's immune system. Since the amount of fluid entering the baby's body is limited during this period, the urine filtered by the kidneys becomes more concentrated. For this reason, the color of the urine in the first days can vary from light yellow to dark yellow or orange. This indicates the importance of monitoring the baby's feeding.

Pink or Brick-Colored Spots in the Diaper: Urate Crystals

If you see pink, orange, or rust/brick-dust-like spots on the diaper, these are often urate crystals (uric acid crystals). Babies accumulate a certain amount of uric acid in their blood while in the womb. After birth, the kidneys begin to excrete this acid from the body. In the first days, since the baby's fluid intake is low, the urine is concentrated, and this uric acid does not fully dissolve, leading to crystallization. As a result, it precipitates on the diaper as “brick dust.”

It is common for these spots to appear on the 3-4 day of life, but this can also be an indicator that the baby is not getting enough fluids. Therefore, when urate crystals are observed, it is important to carefully evaluate the frequency and effectiveness of the baby's feeding. Even in the first days, if there are signs of poor feeding, a doctor should be consulted. It is not possible to distinguish with the naked eye whether the stain is truly blood, so if there is any doubt, consulting a doctor is the safest approach.

Hormonal Discharge in Baby Girls

In baby girls, during the first week after birth, a small amount of mucous, sometimes pink or bloody discharge, may be seen in the diaper due to hormones passed from the mother. This is called “false menstruation” and usually resolves on its own within a few days. This is not a cause for concern. However, if the discharge is excessive, lasts for more than a few days, or if the baby shows other signs of discomfort, it must be evaluated by a doctor.

When Do Normal Urine Volume and Color Return?

Urate crystals and dark urine should be a temporary phase. As breast milk production increases and the baby takes in more fluids, the situation should change rapidly. The main criterion indicating that the baby is getting enough fluids is the number of wet diapers:

  • Day 1: At least 1 wet diaper is expected.
  • Day 2: At least 2 wet diapers are expected.
  • Day 3: At least 3 wet diapers are expected.
  • Day 4: At least 4 wet diapers are expected.
  • After Day 5: The baby should produce at least 6 or more well-soaked diapers within 24 hours. At this stage, urine should be light yellow or almost colorless, and urate crystals should have completely disappeared.

If at any age the baby's urine output is less than expected or feeding is poor, consult a doctor without waiting until day 5.

Baby's Age Number of Wet Diapers (in 24 hours) Urine Color Stool Color/Consistency
Day 1 At least 1 Dark yellow/orange, may contain urate crystals Black, tar-like (meconium)
Day 2 At least 2 Dark yellow/orange, may contain urate crystals Black/dark green (transitional stool)
Day 3 At least 3 Light yellow to dark yellow, urate crystals may decrease Green/yellowish-green (transitional stool)
Day 4 At least 4 Light yellow, urate crystals should be rare Yellow, seedy (breastfed stool)
After Day 5 At least 6+ Light yellow/clear Yellow, seedy (breastfed stool)

When to Seek Emergency Medical Attention?

Some symptoms may indicate a more serious problem and require immediate medical intervention. In the following cases, contact a pediatrician without delay or go to an emergency medical center:

  • Persistent urate crystals: If urate crystals persist after the first 3-4 days or reappear, this is a serious sign that the baby is not getting enough fluids and should be evaluated by a doctor on the same day.
  • Low urine output: If the baby wets fewer than 6 diapers in 24 hours after being 5 days old, or keeps their diaper dry for more than 8 hours at any age.
  • Suspicion of actual blood: If the spots are not powdery but appear as bright red, dripping blood, or if there are blood clots in the urine.
  • Signs of dehydration: If the baby shows symptoms such as excessive sleepiness, lethargy, reluctance to suck, dry mouth and lips, decreased skin elasticity, or a sunken fontanelle on the top of the head.
  • High fever: Especially in babies younger than 3 months, a rectal temperature of 38°C or higher requires urgent medical attention.
  • Symptoms accompanied by jaundice: If the urine color remains consistently dark and at the same time the baby's stool is pale, white, or clay-colored, this may be a sign of jaundice or liver problems.
  • Weight loss: If the baby is not regaining birth weight or weight gain is very slow.

Remember, newborns should not be given any additional fluids (water, tea, sugar water) other than breast milk or formula. These foods fully meet all their fluid needs.

Keep Related Notes in One Place with Anacan

Remembering daily details can be tiring. With Anacan's available tools, you can record the following information and share it more clearly at your next doctor's appointment:

  • Diaper records: Record the time of wet, soiled, and mixed diapers. This information can help the doctor assess feeding but does not alone diagnose dehydration or other illnesses.
  • Feeding records: Record the side and duration of breastfeeding with a timer, and the volume of formula in ml. Duration does not measure the volume of milk consumed; discuss records in conjunction with the baby's weight and clinical assessment.
  • Growth charts: Enter weight, height, and head circumference measurements with the appropriate date and discuss growth dynamics with your pediatrician.

faq.answer: These spots are usually urate crystals. Due to the baby's low fluid intake in the first days, their urine becomes concentrated, and uric acid crystallizes, forming brick-dust-like spots in the diaper. While this is a common occurrence for the first 3-4 days, it can also be a sign that the baby is not feeding enough and requires careful monitoring.
faq.question: What are the brick-colored spots in a newborn's diaper?

faq.answer: Typically, as breast milk production increases, the baby's urine should return to a light yellow or clear color after approximately day 5. At this time, the baby is expected to produce at least 6 or more well-soaked diapers per day. If the urine remains dark or urate crystals are still visible after day 4, consult a doctor.
faq.question: When should the baby's urine return to a normal color?

faq.answer: If urate crystals persist after day 4, if the baby wets fewer than 6 diapers per day after being 5 days old, if you see actual blood in the diaper, if the baby shows signs of dehydration (excessive sleepiness, refusal to feed, dry mouth), or if a baby younger than 3 months has a fever of 38°C or higher, seek immediate medical attention.
faq.question: In which cases should I seek immediate medical attention?

faq.answer: No, babies younger than 6 months, especially newborns, should not be given additional water, tea, or sugar water. Breast milk or formula completely meets all their fluid and nutritional needs. Giving additional fluids can disrupt the baby's feeding and pose a risk to their health.
