articles.title: Exercise During Pregnancy: Safe Activities and Exercises to Avoid
articles.excerpt: Is it dangerous to exercise during pregnancy? Benefits of yoga, swimming, walking, and Kegel exercises. Which sports pose a risk of miscarriage or injury? A safety guide for pregnant women.
articles.content:
After finding out you are pregnant, the first advice from those around you was probably: *"Protect yourself, do not lift heavy, do not move too much, lie down and rest\!"*. In our grandmothers' time, pregnancy was almost treated as a disease, and inactivity was recommended to women.

However, modern medicine has completely changed this approach. We now know that "spending 9 months lying on the couch" is actually harmful to both mother and baby (unless there are specific medical indications). Movement is life, and this holds true during pregnancy as well.

But where is the limit? Which movements are beneficial, and which are dangerous? Let’s turn on the "green" and "red" lights regarding exercise during pregnancy together.Why should you exercise during pregnancy? (Benefits)

If your pregnancy is proceeding without risks (normal), regular exercise will provide you with the following amazing benefits:1.  **Preparation for birth:** Birth is a marathon that requires great physical strength. Exercise trains your muscles and heart for this marathon.
2.  **Weight control:** It prevents excessive weight gain and makes it easier to get back in shape after birth.
3.  **Reduction of pain:** It reduces back and waist pain, as well as constipation and bloating.
4.  **Mood:** Endorphins (happiness hormones) released during exercise reduce stress and improve sleep.
5.  **Risk of gestational diabetes:** It helps regulate blood sugar.Green Light: Which types of exercise are safe? ✅

These sports are considered the "gold standard" for pregnant women because the risk of trauma is minimal and they do not excessively raise the heart rate.1. Walking

It is the simplest, free, and safest exercise. It requires no special equipment.  - **Rule:** Walking for 20-30 minutes a day in the fresh air is sufficient. Make sure you wear comfortable shoes.2. Swimming

It is considered the **most ideal** sport for pregnant women.  - **Why?** Water "takes" your body weight, reducing the load on your joints and back. It eliminates swelling (edema) and cools you down.3. Prenatal Yoga and Pilates

Programs specially prepared for pregnant women keep the body flexible, teach breathing techniques (which will be very necessary during birth!), and calm the mind.  - **Attention:** Make sure your instructor has a certificate for working with pregnancy.4. Kegel exercises

This is an "invisible" exercise that strengthens the pelvic floor muscles.  - **Benefit:** It helps prevent tears during birth and solve urinary incontinence problems after birth. You can do it anywhere (even while sitting).Red Light: What is strictly forbidden? ❌

Pregnancy is not the time to "break records." The following activities can harm the fetus:1. Sports with a risk of falling

During pregnancy, your center of gravity changes and it becomes difficult to maintain balance.  - **Forbidden:** Skiing, horse riding, ice skating, intensive cycling (stationary cycling is okay).2. Contact sports

Stay away from anything where there is a possibility of a blow to your stomach.  - **Forbidden:** Basketball, football, boxing, judo, wrestling.3. Exercises done lying on your back (after the 20th week)

After the 4th month of pregnancy, you should not do crunches or exercise while lying on your back.  - **Reason:** The growing uterus compresses the main blood vessel (inferior vena cava), which causes dizziness and reduced blood flow to the baby.4. "Hot Yoga" and Sauna

Excessive increase in body temperature (hyperthermia) can negatively affect fetal development. Stay away from yoga done in a hot room.5. Jumping and Sudden movements

Your joints soften during pregnancy (thanks to the hormone relaxin). Sharp jumps or twists increase your risk of injury.Golden Rules: What to pay attention to during exercise?1.  **"Talk test":** If you can speak comfortably while exercising, your pace is good. If you are out of breath and cannot speak, the pace is too high; slow down.
2.  **Drink water:** Drink plenty of water before, during, and after exercise. Dehydration can cause uterine contractions.
3.  **Warm-up and Cool-down:** Start movements slowly and end slowly.
4.  **Doctor's permission:** Be sure to consult your doctor before starting exercise.When to stop immediately?

If you feel any of the following symptoms, stop exercising and call your doctor:  - Vaginal bleeding or leaking fluid.
  - Dizziness or blurred vision.
  - Shortness of breath (even while resting).
  - Chest pain.
  - Pain or swelling in the calf.
  - Regular and painful uterine contractions.Exercise during pregnancy is one of the best favors you can do for yourself and your baby. Your goal is not to be an "Olympic champion," but to stay healthy and energetic. Listen to your body, stop when you are tired, and enjoy the movement.

You can use the **Anacan app** to track your daily step count, water intake, and weight. Move with health\!

articles.title: Dental Treatment During Pregnancy: Are Anesthesia and X-rays Harmful to the Baby?
articles.excerpt: What to do about toothache during pregnancy? Do tooth extraction, fillings, anesthesia, and X-rays harm the baby? Important facts you need to know for safe dental treatment.
articles.content:
There is an ancient saying: *"Every child takes a tooth from the mother."* In our grandmothers' time, this was a bitter truth. Due to calcium deficiency and dental fears, women avoided the dentist throughout pregnancy, resulting in tooth loss.

Even today, many pregnant women hesitate to see a doctor even if they have severe toothache. The main source of fear remains the same: *"Will the injection (anesthesia) or X-ray harm my baby?"*.

Enduring pain with this fear is actually more dangerous for your baby than the treatment itself. Let's debunk the myths about dental treatment during pregnancy and look at the medical facts.Why do teeth provide "surprises" during pregnancy?

It is no coincidence that your teeth are more sensitive or your gums bleed during pregnancy.  - **Hormonal Gingivitis:** Increased levels of progesterone and estrogen hormones make gums more sensitive to bacteria. Bleeding, swelling, and redness (pregnancy gingivitis) while brushing teeth is a common occurrence.
  - **The Calcium Myth:** The baby does not "steal" calcium from your teeth. It gets the necessary calcium from your diet (or your bones). Tooth decay is not caused by calcium loss, but by changes in eating habits (cravings for sweets) or gastric acid damaging tooth enamel during morning sickness.Important: Untreated gum infections (periodontitis) increase the risk of premature birth and low birth weight by 7 times. In other words, going to the doctor means protecting your baby!Fear 1: Is anesthesia (numbing injection) harmful?

The biggest fear is: "If an injection is given, the medicine will pass to the baby."

**Medical Fact:** Local anesthesia during pregnancy is **safe**.  - Dentists usually use special anesthetics for pregnant women, such as **Lidocaine**, which contain little or no adrenaline (epinephrine).
  - These drugs pass through the placenta in very minute amounts and do not harm the fetus.
  - **Pain is more dangerous:** The severe stress you experience while in pain increases stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) in your body. This is far more harmful to the baby than a numbing injection.Fear 2: Does an X-ray radiate the baby?

The idea that "X-rays are forbidden, it's radiation!" is a thing of the past.

**Medical Fact:** The radiation dose of **digital X-ray (viziograph)** devices used in modern dentistry is minimal.  - The beam is directed specifically at the oral cavity, not the abdomen.
  - During the procedure, a **lead apron** (protective "apron") is placed over your stomach. This protects your baby 100% from any scattered radiation.
  - Nevertheless, doctors only prescribe X-rays when **absolutely necessary** (e.g., root canal treatment). It is not done for cosmetic purposes.The "Best Time" for the Dentist

Except for emergencies (acute pain, suppuration), planned treatments should take into account the periods of pregnancy:1st Trimester (Not risky, but sensitive)

The baby's organs are forming. You may also experience nausea (toxicosis). During this period, only emergency interventions are performed; planned work is postponed.2nd Trimester (The Golden Period: weeks 14-20)

This is the **most ideal time** to go to the dentist. Organogenesis of the baby is complete, you feel good, and your stomach is not yet large enough to interfere with sitting in the chair. Fillings, dental cleaning, or extractions can be done comfortably during this period.3rd Trimester (Discomfort)

There are no medical contraindications to treatment, but it can be difficult to lie on your back in the dentist's chair for a long time (the inferior vena cava is compressed, causing dizziness).What to avoid?

Some procedures are not recommended during pregnancy:  - **Teeth whitening:** The effects of the chemicals used (peroxide) have not been fully studied. It is advisable to wait until after birth.
  - **Certain antibiotics:** Tetracycline group antibiotics can cause permanent stains on the baby's teeth. Be sure to tell your doctor you are pregnant; they will prescribe safe medications (e.g., Amoxicillin, Erythromycin).
  - **Sedation (Sleeping):** General anesthesia or "laughing gas" is only used if there is a life-threatening emergency.Toothache is not something that should just be "endured." Carrying a source of infection in your mouth is risky for both your health and your baby's.

Tell your doctor that you are **pregnant** and **how many weeks** along you are. They will choose the safest treatment plan for you.

Remember, a happy mother is a mother who brightens her surroundings with her smile. Take care of your teeth!

**Note:** To clarify which medications and procedures are safe during pregnancy, you can check the **"Safety Database" in the Anacan app**.

articles.title: Laser Hair Removal During Pregnancy: Is It Harmful or Should You Wait?
articles.excerpt: Is it safe to have laser hair removal during pregnancy? Do the rays harm the baby? The facts about the effects of Alexandrite and Diode lasers, hormonal hair growth, and the safest hair removal methods for pregnant women.
articles.content:
Changes in your body during pregnancy aren't limited to a growing belly. While many women enjoy thicker hair during this period, an increase in hair ("hirsutism") not just on the head, but also on the face, abdomen, and other unwanted areas can be an unpleasant surprise.

The desire for smooth skin grows, especially in the summer months or as childbirth approaches. If you started laser hair removal before pregnancy, it's natural to want to continue. But are these "miracle rays" safe for your baby? Why are cosmetologists hesitant to accept pregnant clients?

Let's explore the medical facts and risks surrounding laser hair removal.Do laser rays reach the baby?

First, let's dispel the fear of "radiation." The rays used in laser hair removal (Alexandrite, Diode, Nd:YAG) are **non-ionizing** radiation. This means they do not have the power to change cell structure (DNA) like X-rays or CT scans.  - **Depth:** Laser rays penetrate only a few millimeters into the skin (down to the hair follicle).
  - **The Truth:** It is physically impossible for these rays to pass through muscles, enter the uterus, and directly touch the fetus.Nevertheless, most doctors and dermatologists worldwide recommend **abstaining** from laser during pregnancy. But why?Why "Waiting" is the best decision?

Although no direct harm from lasers has been proven, there are very serious reasons not to have this procedure during pregnancy:1. Lack of Research

Science never conducts risky experiments on pregnant women and babies. There are no large-scale clinical studies on the safety of lasers during pregnancy. The phrase "not proven" can mean both "harmless" and "could be harmful." The golden rule in medicine: **When in doubt, don't.**2. Hormonal "Chaos" and Risk of Staining

Melanin (pigment) production increases during pregnancy. This means your skin is more sensitive to light and heat.  - **Risk:** Laser rays can cause permanent burns or **hyperpigmentation** (dark spots) on the skin. Also, due to hormonal influence, your hair may not "obey" the laser—meaning you might be wasting your money.3. Pain and Stress Factor

Laser can be painful, especially in sensitive areas (bikini, underarms). During pregnancy, your pain threshold drops.  - **Danger:** Sharp pain or fear releases adrenaline in the body. This can cause **uterine tone** (contractions), which is undesirable for the course of pregnancy.So, which methods are safe?

Even if you take a break from the laser, you don't have to go ungroomed. Alternatives you can use during pregnancy:✅ Razor (Britva) – The Safest

An old but reliable friend. It contains no chemicals or radiation.  - **Tip:** As your belly grows, it may be difficult to see your lower limbs. Be careful or ask your partner for help.🟡 Sugaring and Waxing (Epilation) – Conditional

If you used these methods before pregnancy and are used to the pain, you can continue.  - **Attention:** Blood vessels dilate during pregnancy. Hot wax or harsh pulling can damage **varicose** veins. Also, pay special attention to hygiene (risk of infection).🟡 Depilatory Creams – With Caution

Although the chemicals in them (barium sulfide, etc.) are absorbed into the blood in minute amounts, the main problem is their sharp smell.  - **Tip:** If you have toxicoses, the smell may cause nausea. Always do an allergy test (on a small part of your arm) before use.When can you return to the laser?

You can resume laser procedures after you hold your baby in your arms.  - **Breastfeeding:** Laser rays do not pass into milk and do not affect the mammary glands (even during underarm epilation). Laser is considered safe for breastfeeding mothers.
  - **However:** Waiting 3-6 months after birth for hormones to fully normalize will ensure more effective results.The saying "beauty requires sacrifice" does not apply to pregnancy. Now the main priority is your comfort and your baby's safety. Laser hair removal isn't going anywhere; it will be waiting for you in 9 months.

For now, prioritize the safest and most stress-free methods. To check your skin's sensitivity and the status of other procedures (e.g., hair dyeing), take a look at the **"Safety Database" in the Anacan app**.

articles.title: Dyeing and Cutting Hair During Pregnancy: Myths and Medical Realities
articles.excerpt: Does cutting hair during pregnancy shorten the baby's life? Does hair dye harm the fetus? Grandmother's myths vs. modern medical answers. Ammonia-free dye, keratin treatments, and safe beauty rules during pregnancy.
articles.content:
After receiving the news of your pregnancy, the time you spend in front of the mirror might be accompanied by a bit of hesitation. Roots that have grown out, split ends that have lost their shape... You want to go to the beauty salon, but the voices of your grandmothers, neighbors, or "scary stories" from the internet echo in your mind: *"Don't cut your hair, the baby's life will be short\!", "Don't dye it, chemicals will pass to the baby\!"*.

Pregnancy is not a period when a woman should stop taking care of herself. On the contrary, being well-groomed to reconcile with your changing body and feel good has a positive impact on your psychology. But where does the myth end and the medical truth begin?

Let's find scientific answers to the most popular questions about hair care and build a safe beauty routine.Myth 1: "You cannot cut your hair during pregnancy"

This is one of the most widespread superstitions in Azerbaijan and many Eastern countries. According to beliefs, cutting hair shortens the baby's life or "cuts" their intelligence.

**Medical Truth:**
This belief has no scientific or biological basis.  - **Hair is lifeless:** The visible part of the hair consists of keratinized (dead) cells. Cutting hair is like cutting nails; it does not create any physiological reaction in your body or the baby in your womb.
  - **Hormonal change:** In fact, during pregnancy, hair does not enter the shedding phase (telogen) due to the effect of the estrogen hormone and becomes thicker. However, if the ends are breaking, cutting them will help the hair look healthier.Conclusion: **You can cut your hair without fear.** This will not affect your baby, only your mood – and in a positive way\!Question 2: Is dyeing hair dangerous?

This issue is a bit more complex because it involves chemical substances.

**Scientific approach:**
The amount of chemicals in hair dyes absorbed into the blood through the skin is very minimal. Most studies conducted show that dyeing hair during pregnancy does not negatively affect the fetus or cause developmental defects.

However, following the principle of **"better safe than sorry,"** doctors recommend adhering to certain rules.1st Trimester Rule: Waiting

The first 12 weeks of pregnancy (1st trimester) are the most sensitive period when the baby's organs are forming. Although the risk has not been proven, most doctors advise refraining from dyeing hair **until the 12th week**.5 Golden Rules for Safe Dyeing (After the 12th week)

If you have decided to dye your hair, follow these safety measures:1.  **Choose ammonia-free dye:** Strong-smelling ammonia vapors can increase your nausea. Prefer organic or plant-based dyes.
2.  **Reduce skin contact:** Try to avoid the dye touching the scalp directly. Techniques like **balayage, ombre, or highlights** are the safest options because the dye is applied only to the hair strands, not the skin.
3.  **Ensure ventilation:** Make sure the salon is well-ventilated. Inhaling chemical odors is harmful.
4.  **Don't extend the time:** Keep the dye on the hair for the minimum time indicated in the instructions.
5.  **Wear gloves:** If you are dyeing it yourself at home, be sure to use gloves.Keratin and Botox: Is straightening allowed?

Hair straightening procedures (Keratin, Botox, Nanoplastica) are usually **not recommended**.  - **Reason:** Many keratin products contain **Formaldehyde** (or substances that turn into formaldehyde when heated). Formaldehyde is a carcinogen and enters the body through the respiratory tract when it evaporates. This is risky for both mother and baby.**Alternative:** Straighten your hair with a blow dryer or reduce frizz by caring for it with natural oils (coconut, argan).Henna and Natural Dyes

If you are concerned about chemical dyes, our grandmothers' method of **Henna** and **Basma** is the safest alternative. Natural henna is completely harmless, strengthens the hair, and gives it shine.  - **Attention:** Stay away from packaged "black hennas," as they may contain chemical additives like PPD (para-phenylenediamine).How will your hair change during pregnancy?

Pregnancy can be the "golden age" of your hair. Many women note that during pregnancy, their hair becomes less oily, shinier, and thicker.  - **Reason:** The estrogen hormone stops the hair loss phase.
  - **After birth:** Unfortunately, 3-4 months after birth, when hormones return to normal, those "saved" hairs will start to shed en masse. This is temporary and transient, do not panic.It is your right to look beautiful during pregnancy, and this is important for your psychological well-being. Cutting hair is completely safe, and dyeing hair is possible within certain rules (after the 12th week, ammonia-free).

Believe in scientific facts, not myths. Every moment you feel happy, you pass happiness hormones to your baby as well.

**Do you have more "Can I/Can't I?" questions?**

articles.title: Drinking Coffee During Pregnancy: Safe Daily Caffeine Limits and Guidelines
articles.excerpt: Is drinking coffee during pregnancy harmful? What is the daily 200 mg caffeine limit? A detailed guide on tea, chocolate, other hidden caffeine sources, effects on the fetus, and safe alternatives.
articles.content:
Do you automatically reach for the coffee machine as soon as you wake up in the morning? Or is an afternoon coffee an indispensable ritual for you to recharge at work? After receiving the news of pregnancy, one of the biggest fears for many women is having to give up their favorite drinks.

If questions like "Should I cut out coffee completely?" or "Is one cup of latte okay?" are worrying you, take a deep breath (or a sip of water). The good news is that you don't have to give up coffee entirely during pregnancy. However, the "golden rule" is still **moderation**.

Let's explore how caffeine affects the baby, what the safe limit is, and how to adjust your daily intake.How does caffeine affect the baby?

When you drink a cup of coffee, caffeine is absorbed into your blood, crosses the placenta, and reaches your baby directly.  - **For you:** Caffeine energizes you, increases heart rate, and speeds up metabolism.
  - **For your baby:** Since the baby's liver is not yet fully developed, it cannot break down caffeine. As a result, caffeine remains in the baby's blood for a long time.High amounts of caffeine can speed up the baby's heart rate, disrupt sleep patterns, and increase activity levels.The Magic Number: 200 mg (milligrams)

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) have set the daily safe caffeine limit for pregnant women at **200 mg**.

So, what does this 200 mg look like in real life?  - **Instant coffee (Nescafe):** 1 cup (200 ml) = \~60-80 mg caffeine. (2 cups a day is fine).
  - **Filter coffee (Brewed):** 1 cup (200 ml) = \~140 mg caffeine. (Limit to 1 cup per day).
  - **Espresso:** 1 shot (30 ml) = \~65 mg caffeine.
  - **Latte / Cappuccino:** Usually made with 1 shot of espresso (\~65-75 mg).Conclusion: Drinking 1 or a maximum of 2 medium-sized cups of coffee a day is completely safe and will not harm your pregnancy.Risks of excessive caffeine

If the daily limit is regularly exceeded (e.g., 4-5 cups a day), it can create the following risks:1.  **Miscarriage risk:** High caffeine intake, especially in the first trimester, can slightly increase the risk of miscarriage.
2.  **Low birth weight:** Caffeine can constrict blood vessels in the placenta, reducing blood flow and nutrition to the baby.
3.  **Iron absorption:** Coffee (and tea) interferes with the absorption of iron from food, which can lead to anemia.Hidden sources of caffeine (Not just coffee!)

Don't relax just because you say "I don't drink coffee." Caffeine hides in our other favorite foods, and they count toward the 200 mg limit:  - **Black tea:** The favorite drink of Azerbaijanis\! 1 glass (armudu) of strong tea contains \~40-50 mg of caffeine. 4 glasses of tea a day already reaches the limit.
  - **Green tea:** Although healthy, 1 cup contains \~30-40 mg of caffeine.
  - **Chocolate:** 50 grams of dark chocolate can contain \~30-40 mg of caffeine.
  - **Cola and carbonated drinks:** 1 can of cola has \~35-40 mg of caffeine.
  - **Energy drinks:** These are strictly **forbidden** during pregnancy because the caffeine content is very high and they contain additional chemicals.Ways to reduce coffee and alternatives

Quitting coffee abruptly can cause headaches and fatigue. Reduce it gradually or try these alternatives:1.  **Decaf Coffee:** The taste is the same, but 97% of the caffeine has been removed. It gives the psychological feeling of "I drank coffee."
2.  **Milk-based drinks:** Drinking coffee with plenty of milk (Latte) reduces the caffeine concentration and increases calcium intake.
3.  **Herbal teas:** Mint, ginger, or rosehip tea are naturally caffeine-free and beneficial. (Note: Some herbs like sage and thyme are not recommended in large quantities).Pregnancy doesn't mean stopping your enjoyment of life. If that cup of coffee you drink on the balcony in the morning brings you happiness, don't give it up. Just prioritize water, ayran, or natural juices for the rest of the day.

To track your caffeine intake and check the safety of other foods, you can use the **"Safety Database" in the Anacan app**. Enjoy\!

articles.title: Headaches during Pregnancy: How to Manage Them Without Medication?
articles.excerpt: Why do headaches occur during pregnancy and how can they be relieved without medication? 5 natural methods for migraines and tension headaches. How to recognize dangerous headaches (preeclampsia)?
articles.content:
Before pregnancy, the solution to a headache was simple: a glass of water and a painkiller. But now, after reading the "Use during pregnancy" section on every medicine box, you hesitantly put the pill back down. "I wonder, could this harm my baby?"

Headaches are a very common complaint during pregnancy. Hormonal storms, changing blood circulation, and lack of sleep can literally make your head "ache." The good news is that in most cases, these pains are harmless, and there is no need to run to the pharmacy to get rid of them.

Let's learn the most effective and natural ways to fight headaches without reaching for painkillers.Why does our head ache more during pregnancy?

Every stage of pregnancy has its own "headache cause":  - **1st Trimester:** The culprits are again hormones. Increased blood volume in your body and the expansion of blood vessels cause headaches. Also, suddenly reducing coffee (caffeine withdrawal) can cause severe pain.
  - **2nd and 3rd Trimester:** Weight gain and changes in posture strain the neck and shoulder muscles. This leads to **"tension-type headaches."**Additionally, dehydration, hunger, stress, and lack of sleep can trigger a headache at any period.5 golden rules for stopping pain without medicine

If you don't want to take paracetamol (or if your doctor doesn't allow it), try these natural methods:1. Water, water, and again water!

The number one cause of headaches during pregnancy is **dehydration**. Sometimes just drinking 1-2 glasses of cool water and waiting 15 minutes can make the pain disappear completely.  - **Tip:** Always carry a water bottle with you during the day. Don't wait until you feel thirsty.2. Hot or Cold Compress

Play with temperature according to the type of pain:  - **For tension pain (Squeezing pain):** Place a **warm** (not hot\!) towel on the back of your neck or shoulders. This will soften tense muscles.
  - **For migraines (Throbbing pain):** Place a **cold** compress (ice pack) on your forehead or temples. Cold narrows dilated vessels and reduces pain.3. "Dark room" therapy

If light and sound bother you (especially during a migraine), drop everything and go to a dark, quiet room. Close your eyes, breathe deeply, and try to sleep for at least 20-30 minutes. Sleep "reboots" the brain.4. Eating in small portions

A drop in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) is the greatest friend of a headache.  - **Solution:** Don't allow a feeling of hunger. Keep walnuts, hazelnuts, dried fruit, or crackers in your bag. Do not eat sweets suddenly after being hungry for a long time; this can cause sugar to spike and then fall again, making the pain worse.5. Massage and Fresh air

Sometimes the root of the pain is hidden in knots in the neck and shoulders. Ask your partner to lightly massage your shoulders and neck. Also, an unventilated room creates an oxygen deficiency. Open a window or go for a short walk. Fresh oxygen is the best medicine.When to rush to the doctor? (Danger signals)

Although headaches are usually harmless, in the second half of pregnancy (after the 20th week), they can be a sign of **Preeclampsia** (Pregnancy toxemia).

Contact your doctor **immediately** in the following cases:  - If the headache starts suddenly and very severely ("The worst pain of my life").
  - If there is blurred vision, "floaters" in front of the eyes, or flashes of light.
  - If sudden swelling has occurred in your face and hands.
  - If there is pain in the upper part of the abdomen (under the ribs).
  - If the pain does not go away despite taking a painkiller (paracetamol).Headaches are one of the tiring parts of pregnancy, but they are your body's way of saying "Rest!" Take care of yourself, drink plenty of water, and reduce stress.

You can use the **Anacan app** to track the frequency and causes (triggers) of headaches. Noting after which food or event the pain occurred will help prevent it in the future.

articles.title: When Can You Learn the Baby's Gender? The Truth About Ultrasound and Blood Tests
articles.excerpt: Boy or girl? The most accurate ways to find out your baby's gender: Ultrasound (USG), NIPT blood test, and folk beliefs. At which week can you get an accurate result and can an ultrasound be wrong?
articles.content:
As soon as you hear the news of your pregnancy, the second question everyone asks (usually right after "congratulations") is typically: *"What is your heart's desire: a Boy or a Girl?"*

Finding out the baby's gender is one of the most exciting stages of pregnancy for parents. Blue or pink? What color should the nursery be decorated in? When to start choosing a name?

While some moms want it to be a surprise, most of us are impatient to uncover this secret as soon as possible. But what does science tell us? When is the earliest and most accurate time to find out the gender? Let’s separate medical methods from our grandmothers' "belly shape" predictions one by one.When is gender biologically determined?

Interestingly, your baby's gender is actually determined at the **exact second** fertilization occurs\! It all depends on the sperm coming from the father:  - If a sperm carrying an **X chromosome** fertilizes the egg, it will be a **GIRL (XX)**.
  - If a sperm carrying a **Y chromosome** fertilizes the egg, it will be a **BOY (XY)**.However, even though everything is genetically ready, it takes time for physical differences (genital organs) to form and become visible on an ultrasound.Method 1: Ultrasound Examination (USM) – The Gold Standard

In Azerbaijan and around the world, ultrasound is the most common and accessible way to find out the baby's gender.When is it visible?  - **Weeks 11-14 (Early probability):** Based on the "Nub theory" (the angle of the genital tubercle), experienced doctors may offer a prediction. However, during this period, girl and boy organs look very similar, so the chance of error is high.
  - **Weeks 16-20 (Accurate result):** This is the ideal time to learn the gender. During the detailed anatomical examination (Doppler) performed at the 20th week, the doctor can clearly see the genital organs.Can an ultrasound be wrong?

Yes, although rare, mistakes do happen.  - **Baby's position:** If the baby has its legs tightly crossed or its back is turned, the doctor may not see anything.
  - **Umbilical cord:** Sometimes the umbilical cord gets caught between the baby's legs and can mistakenly look like a penis.Method 2: NIPT (DNA Blood Test) – Faster, More Accurate

If you don't want to wait until the 16th week, medicine offers a faster way: **Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT)**.  - **How does it work?** During pregnancy, a portion of the baby's DNA passes into the mother's blood. This DNA analysis is performed simply by taking blood from the mother. If a Y chromosome is found in the blood, it's a boy; if not, it's a girl.
  - **When is it done?** From the **10th week** of pregnancy onwards.
  - **Accuracy:** Higher than 99%.
  - **Purpose:** This test is primarily done to check for genetic disorders like Down syndrome; learning the gender is a "bonus" of the test. It is more expensive than an ultrasound.Method 3: Invasive Tests (Amniocentesis)

These tests (sampling of amniotic fluid) provide 100% accurate results, but **they are never performed solely for gender determination**. Because they carry a risk of miscarriage, they are only prescribed by a doctor when there is a serious suspicion of genetic disease.Folk Beliefs and Myths: What do grandmothers say?

Before medicine advanced, people tried to guess the gender using various signs. While these are not scientifically proven, they can be fun:1.  **Belly shape:** "If the belly is pointed (sharp), it's a boy; if it's spread out, it's a girl." (Scientific fact: Belly shape depends on your body structure and muscles).
2.  **Nausea:** "If you vomit a lot in the mornings, it's a girl." (Scientific fact: Some studies suggest that HCG levels are higher in female pregnancies, which may cause more morning sickness, but this is not a definitive rule).
3.  **Appetite:** "If you crave sweets, it's a girl; if you crave salty/sour things, it's a boy."
4.  **Beauty:** "A girl takes away the mother's beauty." (Acne and blemishes).Gender Reveal Party Trend

In recent years, **"Gender Parties"**, which have become popular in Azerbaijan, turn finding out the gender into a celebration. The doctor writes the gender on a piece of paper and puts it in an envelope, and the parents give the envelope to a company that prepares balloons, cakes, or colored smoke. The appearance of blue or pink becomes an unforgettable memory for the family.

While learning the baby's gender is exciting, the most important thing is their health. Whether you find out the result via ultrasound or a blood test, don't forget to allow for a small margin of error (especially with ultrasound).

Boy or girl – it doesn't matter, as long as they are a healthy and blessed child. To track your pregnancy weeks and never miss your ultrasound appointments, you can use the **Anacan app**.

articles.title: Edema in Pregnancy: Causes and Remedies for Swollen Feet
articles.excerpt: Why do legs swell during pregnancy (edema)? How can you distinguish between normal swelling and dangerous symptoms of preeclampsia? 7 effective methods to reduce edema and nutrition tips.
articles.content:
Trying to wear your favorite shoes, but they seem to have shrunk overnight? Do you feel a sense of heaviness and "fullness" in your feet during the evening? Congratulations, you have joined the "Edema Club," experienced by approximately 75% of pregnant women.

Swelling (edema) during pregnancy—specifically the accumulation of fluid in the ankles, feet, and fingers—is very common and usually harmless. However, this condition can sometimes be more than just a cosmetic issue; it can be a serious health signal.

In this article, we will explain the true causes of swelling, ways to get rid of it, and when you should consult a doctor immediately.Why do we "swell" during pregnancy?

Your body's water retention is actually a mechanism that works for the benefit of you and your baby. There are three main physiological reasons for the occurrence of edema:1. Increased blood and fluid volume

During pregnancy, the amount of blood and fluid in your body increases by approximately **50%**. This extra fluid is necessary for the baby's development and serves as a reserve to compensate for the blood you will lose during birth.2. Uterine pressure

As your baby grows, the uterus becomes heavier. This weight puts pressure on the large vein (**inferior vena cava**) that returns blood from the lower body to the heart. As a result, blood circulation slows down, and fluid leaks from the vessels into the tissues, accumulating in the legs.3. Hormonal changes

Increased levels of progesterone and estrogen hormones cause the body to retain salt and water (fluid retention).Interesting fact: Swelling is usually felt more at the end of the day or in hot weather. It typically decreases upon waking up in the morning.Normal edema or a Dangerous signal? (Preeclampsia)

In most cases, swelling is normal. However, sometimes it can be a sign of a serious condition called **Preeclampsia** (Pregnancy toxemia).

**When to see a doctor immediately?**  - **Sudden swelling:** If your face or hands swell suddenly and severely within one day.
  - **Single leg:** If only one leg is swollen, red, and painful (risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis).
  - **Headache and vision disturbances:** If swelling is accompanied by a severe headache, "floaters" in front of the eyes, or blurred vision.
  - **Abdominal pain:** Sharp pain under the ribs.These symptoms can be indicators of preeclampsia accompanied by high blood pressure and require urgent intervention.7 effective ways to reduce edema

If the swelling is physiological, while it may not be possible to eliminate it completely, it can be alleviated.1. Drink more water (Yes, you read that right!)

Though it may seem counterintuitive, drinking water helps flush excess fluid from the body. When the body is dehydrated, it "panics" and stores water as a reserve. Drinking plenty of water (8-10 glasses a day) keeps the kidneys working and washes away toxins.2. Reduce salt, but don't cut it out completely

Salt (sodium) retains water in the body.  - **Avoid:** Pickles (salted cucumber, tomato), brines, chips, salty crackers, and canned goods.
  - **Caution:** You should not cut out salt entirely because iodized salt is important for the baby. Simply reduce the amount and do not sprinkle extra salt on food at the table.3. Sleep on your left side

Lying on your left side while sleeping relieves the "inferior vena cava" from the pressure of the uterus. This improves blood circulation and makes the kidneys' job easier.4. Elevate your legs

Whenever you find the opportunity during the day, and especially in the evenings, raise your legs above heart level. Lie on the sofa and put a pillow under your feet or lean your legs against the wall. Gravity will help the fluid return.5. Cabbage leaf compress (Grandmother's method)

For a natural cooling effect, you can wrap chilled cabbage leaves from the refrigerator around your swollen legs. This reduces the sensation of pain and heat.6. Comfortable shoes and socks  - Completely avoid high-heeled shoes.
  - Do not wear socks with tight elastic that constrict your legs.
  - If your doctor recommends them, wear **compression stockings (varicose vein socks)**. They should be put on in the morning before getting out of bed.7. Stay active

Do not stay in the same position (sitting or standing) for long periods.  - If you work in an office, get up and walk every hour.
  - Rotate your ankles in circular motions.
  - Swimming or walking in water is the best exercise for edema due to the water pressure.Nutrition: Natural remedies to fight edema

Some foods have a natural diuretic effect and can reduce swelling:  - **Potassium-rich foods:** Bananas, apricots (dried apricots), potatoes (baked with skin), spinach.
  - **Natural diuretics:** Cucumber, watermelon (in season), celery, parsley (in small amounts).
  - **Protein:** A lack of protein (meat, eggs, legumes) in the diet can also cause edema.Having "elephant feet" during pregnancy is no one's dream, but it is a temporary condition. Shortly after birth (usually within the first 1-2 weeks), your body will rapidly shed that excess fluid, and you will be able to wear your old shoes again.

Use the **Anacan app** to track your weight gain and swelling symptoms. If the scale shows a sudden increase, this could be a sign of hidden edema—inform your doctor immediately.

articles.title: Iron Deficiency (Anemia) in Pregnancy: How to Overcome Iron Deficiency?
articles.excerpt: Why does anemia occur during pregnancy? Recognize symptoms like fatigue, dizziness, and paleness. Learn about proper nutrition and treatment methods to overcome iron deficiency.
articles.content:
It is normal to feel tired during pregnancy. But what if this fatigue reaches the point where you are out of breath while climbing stairs or don't want to get out of bed in the morning? Maybe it's not just "pregnancy fatigue," it could be **Anemia** (Iron Deficiency).

Approximately 40% of pregnant women worldwide suffer from iron deficiency anemia. This means your body does not have enough healthy red blood cells (erythrocytes). The good news is that this condition is easily diagnosed and can be completely eliminated with the right approach.

Let's learn ways to get your energy back and provide your baby with full oxygen.Why does our "blood decrease" during pregnancy?

In fact, the amount of blood in your body does not decrease during pregnancy; on the contrary, it **increases**. Blood volume increases by approximately 50% to nourish the baby.

But there is a "trick" here: the liquid part of the blood (plasma) increases faster than the red blood cells. As a result, the blood becomes somewhat "diluted." This is physiological anemia and is normal. But if your body does not have enough **iron** stores to create additional red blood cells (especially in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters), then real anemia occurs. The baby takes the iron it needs from the mother, and the mother is left without reserves.The Hidden Enemy: Symptoms of Anemia

Sometimes symptoms are so mild that women accept them as a natural part of pregnancy. However, pay attention to the following signs:  - **Extreme weakness and fatigue.**
  - **Dizziness:** Especially when standing up suddenly.
  - **Shortness of breath:** Even if you move a little.
  - **Pallor:** In the skin, lips, and nail beds.
  - **Palpitations:** Frequent fluttering of the heart (Tachycardia).
  - **Cold hands and feet.**
  - **Strange cravings (Pica):** Some women have a desire to eat ice, chalk, soil, or raw rice.Risks for Baby and Mother

Untreated severe anemia can lead to several complications:1.  **Preterm birth or low birth weight:** The baby may suffer from growth restriction when it does not receive enough oxygen.
2.  **Postpartum depression:** It becomes more difficult for mothers with anemia to recover after birth, and the risk of depression increases.
3.  **Risk of bleeding:** It becomes difficult to compensate for the blood lost during delivery.How to Increase Iron? (Golden Rules)

"Iron discipline" is needed to prevent or treat anemia.1. "Iron Table": What to eat?

Iron in food comes in two types: **Heme (Animal origin)** and **Non-heme (Plant origin)**. Heme iron is more easily absorbed by the body.  - **Best sources:** Red meat (beef), liver (1-2 times a month), chicken, fish.
  - **Plant sources:** Lentils, chickpeas, spinach, dried apricots, raisins, pomegranate, walnuts/hazelnuts, beets.Tip: Lentil soup or bean stew with meat, favorite dishes of Azerbaijani cuisine, are excellent sources of iron!2. Friends of Iron (Vitamin C)

To increase iron absorption, be sure to combine it with Vitamin C.  - Eat a **tomato salad** with your meat dish.
  - Squeeze **lemon** on lentils.
  - Take your iron pill with orange juice.3. Enemies of Iron (Tea and Calcium)

Our biggest mistake is drinking "steeped tea" immediately after a meal.  - **Tannins:** Substances in tea and coffee reduce iron absorption by 50-60%. Drink tea **at least 1 hour after** a meal.
  - **Calcium:** Milk, yogurt, and cheese hinder iron absorption. Try not to mix meat dishes with dairy products (except ayran). If you are taking a calcium supplement, take it at a different time from your iron supplement.Iron Supplements: When and How?

Often, nutrition alone is not enough, and your doctor prescribes iron pills (supplements).  - **How to take:** For best results, take on an empty stomach or 2 hours after a meal with water or fruit juice.
  - **Side effects:** Constipation, nausea, or darkening of stool color is normal. If constipation occurs, drink plenty of water and eat high-fiber foods (apricots, plums).Anemia should not be the "nightmare" of pregnancy. With a timely blood test (checking Hemoglobin and Ferritin) and proper nutrition, you will both feel vigorous and give your baby a healthy start.

If you feel weak, do not ignore it by saying "it's pregnancy, it will pass." Be sure to consult your doctor.

articles.title: Gestational Diabetes (Pregnancy Diabetes): Symptoms, Diet, and Control
articles.excerpt: What is gestational diabetes and does it affect the baby? Essential information on hidden symptoms, glucose tolerance tests, healthy diet guidelines, and managing insulin treatment.
articles.content:
When your doctor tells you during pregnancy, "You have gestational diabetes," your first reaction might be fear or guilt. Questions like "Did I eat too much candy?" or "Will something happen to my baby?" might spin in your head.

Stay calm. Gestational diabetes (or pregnancy sugar as it's commonly known) is a very common condition occurring in about 10% of pregnant women. This diagnosis doesn't mean you're a "bad mother" or necessarily a sweets addict. It is simply your body's reaction to pregnancy hormones.

The good news is that with proper control and nutrition, you can have a completely healthy pregnancy and give birth to a healthy baby. Let's explore the solutions to this "sweet" problem together.

What is gestational diabetes and why does it occur?

Normally, when we eat, blood sugar levels rise and the pancreas secretes insulin. Insulin acts as a "key" that allows sugar to enter cells and be converted into energy.

During pregnancy, the placenta produces various hormones for the baby's development. However, these hormones sometimes interfere with the work of insulin (this is called insulin resistance). The mother's pancreas must produce more insulin to compensate for this situation. If the body cannot produce enough insulin, blood sugar levels rise and gestational diabetes occurs.

Symptoms: How does it manifest?

The most insidious part of gestational diabetes is that it often shows no symptoms. A woman may feel completely normal. However, when sugar levels are very high, the following symptoms may be observed:

  • Unbearable thirst: A constant desire to drink water.

  • Frequent urination: While this is normal in pregnancy, it becomes more intense during diabetes.

  • Dry mouth.

  • Fatigue.

Because it often goes unnoticed, a "Glucose Tolerance Test" (OGTT) is recommended for all pregnant women between 24-28 weeks of pregnancy. This test is the only accurate way to make a diagnosis.

What are the risks for the baby?

If sugar is not kept under control, it can pose some risks for both mother and baby:

  • Large fetus (Macrosomia): Excess sugar in the mother's blood passes to the baby. The baby's body produces a lot of insulin in response, which causes rapid weight gain (especially in the shoulder and abdominal area). Babies heavier than 4 kg can have a difficult birth.

  • Premature birth: High sugar can cause an increase in amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios) and early contractions.

  • Postpartum hypoglycemia: Immediately after birth, the baby's blood sugar can drop suddenly (because they were used to high sugar in the womb).

  • Future risk: These children have a slightly higher risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes in the future.

Remember: These risks only arise when sugar remains uncontrolled. Babies of mothers who follow their diet are usually born completely healthy.

>

The basis of treatment: Nutrition and Diet

80-90% of women with gestational diabetes can maintain normal sugar levels through proper nutrition alone, without the need for medication. Here are the main rules:

1. Choose carbohydrates wisely

Sugar cannot be cut out completely because the baby needs energy for development. However, you must replace "bad" carbohydrates with "good" ones.

  • ⛔ Stay away (Simple carbohydrates): White bread, white rice (pilaf), sugar, cakes, cookies, sugary sodas, fruit juices. These spike sugar suddenly.

  • ✅ Accept (Complex carbohydrates): Whole wheat bread, buckwheat, bulgur, oats, legumes (lentils, chickpeas). These are absorbed slowly into the blood.

2. Eat frequently and in small portions

Instead of 3 large meals a day, have 3 main meals and 2-3 snacks (interim meals). This prevents sharp fluctuations in blood sugar.

3. Protein and Vegetables are your friends

Every meal should include protein (meat, fish, eggs, cottage cheese) and plenty of vegetables (cucumber, tomato, greens, cabbage). Fibrous vegetables slow down the absorption of sugar into the blood.

4. Pay attention to fruits

Fruits are beneficial but contain sugar.

  • Stay away from grapes, figs, melons, and watermelons (they have too much sugar).

  • Prefer apples, pears, oranges, and berries (strawberries, raspberries).

  • Don't eat fruit alone; eat it with a handful of walnuts or a slice of cheese (protein reduces the effect of sugar).

How to measure sugar? (Glucometer)

Your doctor will ask you to measure your sugar at home. For this, you should buy a small device – a glucometer.

  • Morning fasting: The norm should usually be below 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/l).

  • 1 hour after a meal: Below 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/l).

  • 2 hours after a meal: Below 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/l).

(Target numbers may vary according to your doctor).

If the need for insulin arises...

If sugar does not drop despite the diet, your doctor may prescribe insulin injections or pills. Do not be afraid of this at all.

  • Insulin does not cross the placenta and does not harm the baby.

  • This does not mean you are "incapable"; your placenta is simply producing very strong hormones.

  • Insulin is temporary and will be stopped after birth.

What happens after birth?

Good news: As soon as the baby is born, the placenta is expelled from the body and diabetes usually disappears immediately. However, your doctor will want to check you again 6-12 weeks after delivery.

Gestational diabetes is a warning bell, but not a sentence. It can be turned into an opportunity that forces you to eat healthier and monitor your weight throughout pregnancy. As a result, both you stay in shape and your baby develops healthily.

You can use the Anacan app to track your nutrition regimen, monitor weight gain, and record your sugar measurements. May you hold your baby in health!

articles.title: 7 Natural Ways to Relieve Morning Sickness and Pregnancy Toxicosish
articles.excerpt: Tired of morning sickness? 7 effective and natural ways to combat toxemia during pregnancy. A comprehensive guide on ginger, proper nutrition, and home remedies for relief.
articles.content:
Although the news of pregnancy brings great joy, for many women, this joy is overshadowed by the famous "morning sickness" (toxicosis). Although it is called "morning," it can actually catch you at any time of the day – at work, while cooking, or in bed at night.

Every woman's experience with toxicosis is different: some experience only a slight feeling of nausea, while others cannot get out of bed for days. The good news is that this condition is usually a sign that the pregnancy is progressing healthily (hormones are at work!) and it goes away on its own by the 12th-14th week.

But how to endure it until then? How can you help yourself with simple remedies in your kitchen without resorting to medication? Let's look at 7 proven natural ways to combat toxicosis.

Why does toxicosis occur?

Although the exact cause is not fully known, hormones are to blame again. In the first months of pregnancy, the rapid increase in the HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) hormone and the rise in Estrogen levels slow down the digestive system and sharpen the sense of smell. This causes nausea.

In addition, a drop in blood sugar and stress can also worsen symptoms.

7 Golden Rules to Reduce Nausea

1. Never leave your stomach empty

The biggest mistake is refusing to eat for fear of nausea. When the stomach is empty, stomach acid irritates the walls and increases nausea.

  • Solution: Instead of eating large portions 3 times a day, eat small amounts 5-6 times. Always carry crackers, dried fruit, or nuts with you.

2. Have a snack before getting out of bed in the morning

Blood sugar is low when you wake up in the morning, which triggers nausea.

  • Solution: Before going to bed in the evening, put some salty cookies, crackers, or rusks on your bedside table (nightstand). As soon as you wake up, before even getting out of bed, eat 1-2 pieces and lie down for 10-15 minutes. This will soothe your stomach.

3. Ginger – Nature's most powerful weapon

Ginger has been used for centuries against motion sickness and nausea. Scientific studies have proven that it is also effective in pregnancy toxicosis.

  • How to use: Grate fresh ginger and add it to your tea, suck on ginger candies, or simply chew a slice.

4. Lemon and sour flavors

Have you ever wondered why pregnant women love pickles? Sour tastes and smells soothe the nausea center.

  • Solution: Put a slice of lemon in your water. When you feel nauseous, smell a freshly cut lemon. Sour foods like fruit leather or cornelian cherry can also help.

5. Pay attention to fluid intake

Dehydration makes toxicosis even worse. However, drinking too much water at once can fill your stomach and make you vomit.

  • Solution: Drink water in sips throughout the day. If plain water makes you nauseous, try mineral water, mint tea, or compote. Drinking ice water works better for some women.

6. Avoid irritating odors

During this period, your nose works like a "police dog." The smell of fried onions, heavy perfumes, or cleaning products can be unbearable.

  • Solution: Eat meals cold (cold food has less odor). Ventilate the kitchen frequently. Use light scents that you enjoy (e.g., mint or lemon oil).

7. Vitamin B6

In some cases, doctors recommend Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplements to reduce nausea.

  • Food sources: Bananas, avocados, chicken, and hazelnuts are rich in B6. Be sure to consult your doctor before taking it as a medication.

When to see a doctor?

Although toxicosis is uncomfortable, it is usually safe. However, in rare cases, a severe form called Hyperemesis Gravidarum can develop. If you experience the following situations, be sure to go to the doctor:

  • If you cannot consume any food or liquid within 24 hours.

  • If you vomit more than 3-4 times a day.

  • If your weight is decreasing rapidly.

  • If the color of your urine has darkened and its amount has decreased (a sign of dehydration).

  • If there is dizziness and fainting.

Combating toxicosis requires patience. Remember that this period is temporary and every nausea brings you one step closer to your baby. Be kind to yourself, rest as much as possible, and listen to your body's needs.

To track your symptoms, set up your nutrition plan, and benefit from the experiences of other mothers, download the Anacan app. We wish you a healthy pregnancy!

articles.title: Uterine Hypertonus (Hypertonicity): Is It Dangerous and How Is It Treated?
articles.excerpt: What is "uterine tone" (hypertonus) during pregnancy? Causes of abdominal tightening and cramps, dangerous situations, and treatment options. Everything you need to know about Magnesium, Papaverine, and bed rest.
articles.content:
One of the most common and concerning diagnoses women hear in the doctor's office during pregnancy is "Uterine tone" or "Hypertonus." When a doctor frowns during an ultrasound and says, "You have tone," it becomes an alarm signal for many expectant mothers.

But what actually is this "tone"? Does every abdominal tightening result in a miscarriage? Or is it a natural reaction of the body? Let's explore the truths, myths, and medical facts behind this popular diagnosis.

What is uterine tone, actually?

In simple terms, the uterus (womb) is a hollow, muscular organ. Like every muscle (for example, a representative arm muscle), the uterus has the ability to contract and relax.

  • Normal Tone: It is normal for the uterine muscle to be under slight tension.

  • Hypertonus (High Tone): This is the premature, involuntary, and prolonged contraction of the uterine muscles.

Throughout pregnancy, as the uterus grows, the muscle fibers stretch. Sometimes, the uterus may contract for a short period while walking, laughing, or when the fetus moves. This is a natural occurrence. However, if these contractions are painful and last a long time, one should be careful.

Symptoms: How can you feel the tone?

Many women describe tone as "turning to stone."

  • Abdominal hardening: When you place your hand on your stomach, you feel it is as hard as a rock.

  • Pain: Dull or pulling pains similar to menstrual cramps, starting from the lower back and radiating to the lower abdomen.

  • Feeling of heaviness: A sense of pressure or fullness in the groin area.

Why does it occur? (Causes)

Many factors can cause hypertonus:

  • Progesterone deficiency: A lack of this hormone, which protects the pregnancy, can prevent the uterus from relaxing.

  • Magnesium deficiency: Magnesium is essential for muscle relaxation.

  • Stress and fatigue: Nervous tension directly affects the muscles.

  • Physical exertion: Lifting heavy objects or standing for long periods.

  • Infections: Sexually transmitted infections or kidney problems.

  • Gas and bloating: Intestinal problems can create tone by putting pressure on the uterus.

When is tone dangerous?

Not every abdominal tightening is scary. However, in the following cases, it can create a risk of miscarriage or preterm labor:

  • In the early weeks (1st trimester): Tone accompanied by severe pain or spotting can cause the embryo to detach from the uterine wall (hematoma).

  • In later weeks: If contractions become regular and do not subside with rest, this can lead to shortening of the cervix and premature birth.

Don't Mistake It for Braxton Hicks (False Labor)!

Painless, irregular, and short-lived (30-60 seconds) contractions starting after the 20th week are "false labor." This is the uterus practicing for birth and is completely normal.

>

Treatment and First Aid: What to do?

If you feel tension in your abdomen, do not panic immediately. Stress increases tone even further.

First Aid at Home (Before the doctor)

  • Lie down and rest: Stop moving and take a comfortable position.

  • Drink water: Dehydration is one of the main causes of muscle spasms. Drink 1-2 glasses of water.

  • Take deep breaths: Inhale deeply through your nose and exhale slowly through your mouth. This relaxes the body.

  • Warm shower: Warm water (not hot!) can soften the muscles.

Medical Treatment (Only with a doctor's prescription!)

In Azerbaijan, doctors usually prescribe the following agents during hypertonus:

  • Magnesium B6: To calm the muscles and strengthen the nervous system.

  • Spasmolytics (Papaverine suppositories, No-spa): "Emergency" tools to eliminate pain and spasms.

  • Progesterone preparations (Duphaston, Utrogestan): If the cause is hormonal deficiency.

Attention: Do not take any medication, even vitamins, without consulting your doctor.

>

The diagnosis of "uterine tone" should not scare you, but it should not be ignored either. Listen to your body. If your pains are severe, if there is bleeding, or if you are simply worried, be sure to contact your doctor.

For your pregnancy to pass calmly and without stress, record your daily symptoms in the Anacan app and benefit from the advice in the "Safety" section. Remember, a calm mother means a healthy baby.

articles.title: Weight Gain During Pregnancy: Normal Ranges and Tips for Prevention
articles.excerpt: How much weight gain is normal during pregnancy? Learn about the ideal weight gain chart based on BMI, risks of excess weight, and the truth about the eat for two myth.
articles.content:
After receiving the news of pregnancy, everyone around you starts offering you food: "Eat, dear, you're eating for two now!". While this sentence sounds pleasant (especially if there's a delicious cake in front of you), modern medicine says the exact opposite.

Seeing the numbers increase every time you step on the scale is a source of joy for some mothers and stress for others. It is natural for your body to change and round out, but where does the limit end? Which numbers are considered healthy and which are risky?

In this article, we explored the scientific norms of ideal weight gain during pregnancy, where those kilograms actually go, and how you can maintain your healthy shape.

How much should ideal weight gain be? (BMI Chart)

Every woman is different, and there is no "single norm for everyone." How much weight you should gain depends on your pre-pregnancy weight and height, i.e., your Body Mass Index (BMI).

The recommendations of international medical institutions (IOM) are as follows:

| Pre-pregnancy status | BMI | Ideal Weight Gain |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Underweight | Less than 18.5 | 12.5 – 18 kg |

| Normal weight | 18.5 – 24.9 | 11.5 – 16 kg |

| Overweight | 25.0 – 29.9 | 7 – 11.5 kg |

| Obese | 30.0 and above | 5 – 9 kg |

| Twin pregnancy | - | 16 – 24 kq |

Note: Trying to lose weight during pregnancy (even if you are overweight) is not recommended. The goal is to keep weight gain under control.

>

Where do these kilos go? (Mathematical calculation)

Often women think that all 15 kilograms they gain are fat. Fortunately, this is not the case! The weight you gain is actually spent on the "life support system" needed to nourish and protect the baby.

The breakdown of an average 13-14 kg weight gain is approximately as follows:

  • Baby: ~3.5 kg

  • Placenta: ~0.7 kg

  • Amniotic fluid: ~1 kg

  • Uterus (Enlarged organ): ~1 kg

  • Breasts: ~1 kg

  • Increased blood volume: ~1.5 kg

  • Body fluids (Swelling): ~1.5 kg

  • Fat stores (Energy for birth and breastfeeding): ~3-4 kg

As you can see, most of this weight will go away immediately after birth and in the first few weeks.

The "Eating for Two" Myth

The biggest misconception is thinking that a pregnant woman needs double the calories.

  • 1st Trimester: There is NO need for extra calories. Normal nutrition is sufficient.

  • 2nd Trimester: Approximately +340 kcal should be added daily (this just means a sandwich or a bowl of yogurt).

  • 3rd Trimester: Approximately +450 kcal daily (about as much as a healthy snack).

That is, you need to eat not for two people, but for (quality for) two people.

Risks of Excessive Weight Gain

Gaining more weight than the norm is not just an aesthetic problem; it can pose serious risks for both mother and baby:

  • Gestational Diabetes: The risk of pregnancy diabetes increases.

  • Preeclampsia: High blood pressure and protein leakage.

  • Large fetus (Macrosomia): A baby weighing more than 4 kg can make delivery difficult.

  • Cesarean possibility: The risk of surgical intervention increases due to a large fetus or complications.

  • Postpartum difficulty: It becomes harder to lose the extra pounds.

5 Golden Rules for Healthy Weight Gain

How can you maintain your weight without going hungry and leaving the baby without vitamins?

1. Avoid "empty" calories

Sugary drinks, packaged sweets, fast food... These give you energy, but they are of no benefit to the baby. When you crave sweets, eat fruit, dried fruit, or dark chocolate.

2. Choose complex carbohydrates

Choose whole wheat bread instead of white bread, buckwheat or bulgur instead of white rice. These foods keep blood sugar stable and keep you full for longer.

3. Stay active

Pregnancy is not an illness! If your doctor allows, walking for 20-30 minutes a day, swimming, or doing pregnancy yoga speeds up metabolism.

4. Water regimen

Sometimes our bodies mistake thirst for hunger. Drinking plenty of water throughout the day both regulates appetite and prevents swelling (edema).

5. Regular monitoring (Anacan App)

Weigh yourself on the same day and at the same time (on an empty stomach in the morning) every week. Monitor your chart using the "Weight Tracker" function in the Anacan app. The app will immediately show you whether your weight is within the norm.

Weight gain during pregnancy is inevitable and necessary. The main point is not to get stuck on the numbers, but to pay attention to the quality of the food you eat. Your body is doing a magnificent job — respect it and support it with healthy foods.

If you cannot control your appetite or if your weight is increasing rapidly, be sure to consult your doctor. Balance is the best key for a healthy mother and a healthy baby.

articles.title: How to Calculate Due Date? Why Last Menstrual Period (LMP) Matters
articles.excerpt: When will your baby be born? A detailed guide on the most accurate ways to calculate your due date, the importance of the Last Menstrual Period (LMP), and Naegele's rule. Use our due date calculator for precision.
articles.content:
As soon as they see a positive result on a pregnancy test, the first question that comes to every future mother's mind is the same: "When will I hold my baby in my arms?"

Knowing this magical date is important not only for preparing the nursery or planning maternity leave, but also for medically monitoring the progress of the pregnancy. However, this date often causes confusion. Why do doctors calculate pregnancy from the date of the last period rather than the day of conception? How many months is 40 weeks actually?

Let's explain the logic behind these calculations and how you can find out the most accurate birth date in simple language.

Why is "Last Menstrual Period" (LMP) so important?

Many women try to calculate the week of pregnancy from the day they think conception occurred (the day of sexual intercourse). However, your doctor will always ask for the First Day of your Last Menstrual Period (LMP).

The reason for this is simple:

  • It is difficult to know the exact day: Conception may not occur on the day of intercourse. Sperm can live in the female body for up to 5 days. That is, if you had intercourse on Sunday, conception may have occurred on Wednesday.

  • Medical standard: The first day of the period is a precise reference point. In medicine, pregnancy is accepted as 40 weeks (280 days) and this period is calculated starting from the LMP.

This means that in the first two weeks of your pregnancy, you are technically not pregnant yet! Your body is simply preparing for ovulation.

How is the due date calculated? (Naegele's Rule)

The most popular formula used by doctors (and our app) is Naegele's Rule. You can easily calculate this yourself:

Formula: First day of your last period + 7 days - 3 months + 1 year.

>

Example:

Suppose the first day of your last period was November 1, 2025.

  • Add 7 days: November 8.

  • Go back 3 months: August 8.

  • Add 1 year: August 8, 2026.

Estimated Due Date: August 8, 2026.

This method works quite accurately for women with a regular 28-day menstrual cycle.

What if your cycle is irregular?

If your menstrual cycle is shorter or longer than 28 days (for example, 35-40 days), Naegele's rule may be slightly inaccurate. In such cases, the most reliable method is an Early Ultrasound Scan (USG).

  • Dating Scan: An ultrasound performed between the 8th and 13th weeks of pregnancy determines the pregnancy week with the highest accuracy (with an error of 3-5 days) by measuring the baby's crown-rump length (CRL).

  • If there is a difference of more than 7 days between the ultrasound date and your calculated LMP date, the doctor usually takes the ultrasound date as the basis and adjusts the due date ("corrected date").

The due date is an estimate, not a "deadline"!

Knowing this will save you from unnecessary stress: only 4-5% of women give birth on the calculated day.

Even if your baby is born:

  • 2 weeks early (38th week) or

  • 2 weeks late (42nd week),

it is considered a completely normal and full-term birth.

The due date just gives you a "target window." The baby may have their own plans!

Make it easier with the Anacan App

Don't waste time holding a calendar and counting days. The "Due Date Calculator" in the Anacan app takes care of everything for you.

  • Download the app.

  • Enter the first day of your last period.

  • The system will immediately show you the estimated due date, which week you are currently in, and your baby's zodiac sign.

Knowing the due date is important for monitoring your pregnancy, performing screening tests on time, and evaluating the baby's development. However, do not look at this date as an "exam day." Your baby will come when they are ready.

Your task is to enjoy every moment of this 40-week journey and listen to your body. Wishing you a healthy delivery!

articles.title: Pregnancy Week-by-Week: A Comprehensive Guide to All 40 Weeks
articles.excerpt: A 40-week pregnancy journey: Baby development by trimester, changes in the mother's body, and essential medical advice. Your week-by-week pregnancy calendar guide for this miraculous path.
articles.content:
Pregnancy is the longest, most difficult, yet most unforgettable journey a woman can experience in her life. During 9 months (or more precisely, 40 weeks), your body literally creates a miracle. Although days may sometimes seem to pass very slowly, incredible changes are happening inside you every second.

"How big is my baby now?", "Why do I feel this way?", "What will happen this week?" are likely questions on your mind. In this detailed guide, we have mapped out this adventure for you by dividing your pregnancy into trimesters and weeks.

First Trimester: The Invisible Revolution (Weeks 1-13)

This period is the most critical and sensitive stage where the foundation is laid. Even if you don't look pregnant outwardly yet, a "hormonal storm" is ruling your body.

Weeks 1-4: The Beginning of Everything

The pregnancy calendar is calculated from the first day of your last period. This means you aren't actually pregnant during the first two weeks!

  • What's happening? Ovulation, fertilization, and the implantation of the cell into the uterus.

  • You: You might not feel anything at all, though sometimes light spotting occurs. It's too early for a test.

Weeks 5-8: Heartbeat

Your baby is now called an "embryo" and is developing rapidly.

  • Baby: The heart begins to beat (100-160 beats per minute!). The brain, spinal column, eyes, and ears are forming. At 8 weeks, it is the size of a raspberry seed.

  • You: "Welcome, morning sickness!" Nausea, fatigue, and breast tenderness reach their peak. It's time for your first ultrasound appointment.

Weeks 9-13: Human Form

The embryonic period ends; it is now a "fetus."

  • Baby: Fingers separate, and nails form. The baby begins to move (though you can't feel it yet). Genitals are forming. At 12 weeks, it is the size of a lemon.

  • You: Your waistline may thicken as the uterus grows. The important "Double Test" (screening) is performed at 12 weeks. Nausea usually subsides by the end of the trimester.

Second Trimester: The "Golden Era" (Weeks 14-27)

For many women, this is the most comfortable period of pregnancy. Your energy returns, your belly begins to show in a sweet way, and that magnificent moment arrives — the first kick!

Weeks 14-17: Rapid Growth

  • Baby: Bones are hardening, and the skin is thin and transparent. It can make facial expressions (frowning, smiling). At 16 weeks, it is the size of an avocado.

  • You: Your appetite increases. Nosebleeds and gum sensitivity may occur (due to increased blood circulation). Are you impatient to learn the gender? There isn't much longer to go!

Weeks 18-22: Life Felt

  • Baby: Hearing develops — it hears your voice and your heartbeat. Movements become stronger. At 20 weeks, it is the size of a banana.

  • You: You feel the first movements (quickening) — like butterflies fluttering in your stomach. Between weeks 20-22, a detailed anatomical ultrasound ("Doppler") is performed to check all the baby's organs.

Weeks 23-27: Viability

  • Baby: Lungs are preparing to breathe. It can open and close its eyes. The sense of taste develops. At 27 weeks, it is the size of a cauliflower.

  • You: Your belly grows rapidly, and stretch marks may appear (don't neglect moisturizing!). Heartburn and leg cramps might bother you. The glucose loading test is performed during this period.

Third Trimester: Final Preparations (Weeks 28-40)

The finish line is in sight! Your baby is preparing to come into the world, and you are focusing on birth both physically and emotionally.

Weeks 28-32: Time to Gain Weight

  • Baby: The brain develops rapidly. A subcutaneous layer of fat forms, and the baby "rounds out." It can open its eyes enough to react to light. At 32 weeks, it is the size of a butternut squash.

  • You: Sleeping becomes difficult, and you may feel shortness of breath (as the uterus presses against the diaphragm). False contractions (Braxton Hicks) may start — your body is practicing.

Weeks 33-36: Immunity and Position

  • Baby: It gains immunity by receiving your antibodies. Bones (except for the skull) harden completely. It begins to take the birth position (head down). At 36 weeks, it is the size of a melon.

  • You: Breathing becomes easier as the baby drops lower, but the need to go to the toilet increases. It's the perfect time to prepare your hospital bag!

Weeks 37-40+: Meeting Time!

The pregnancy is now considered "full term."

  • Baby: Organs are fully ready. The hair covering the body (lanugo) falls off. Weight varies between 3-4 kg. It is the size of a watermelon and is waiting for you.

  • You: Your water could break or contractions could start at any moment. The cervical plug (bloody show) may appear. Be patient; nature knows its job.

This 40-week marathon is sometimes tiring, sometimes painful, but a process whose result is worth the world. Every woman's and every pregnancy's story is different. Don't compare yourself to others; believe in the power of your body.

Don't forget to download the Anacan app to track your baby's weekly development, note your symptoms, and be fully prepared for birth.

Wishing you a healthy delivery!

articles.title: Unplanned Pregnancy: First Steps and Psychological Preparation
articles.excerpt: What to do when pregnancy news is unexpected? Dealing with the initial shock, mixed emotions, and psychological preparation for the future. Steps to accept an unplanned pregnancy and ensure a healthy start.
articles.content:
Life sometimes presents us with its biggest surprises when we least expect them. Seeing those two red lines on a test you bought from the pharmacy... If this wasn't in your plans, your first reaction might be shock, fear, or even panic rather than joy. It is completely natural for thoughts like "I'm not ready for this!", "What will happen to my job?", and "Now was not the time" to swirl in your head.

An unplanned pregnancy can be one of the most powerful emotional shocks in a woman's life. However, it is important to remember that being "unplanned" does not mean it is "unwanted" or won't have a "happy ending." Many great stories begin with unexpected starts.

In this article, we have compiled the first steps you should take, from how to overcome the initial shock to talking with your partner and medical check-ups.

Step 1: Accept your feelings (Shock is normal!)

Society instills in us that news of pregnancy should always be met with immediate tears of joy. However, reality is different.

  • Mixed emotions: You may feel joy, fear, guilt, and excitement all at the same time. Do not blame yourself. It is normal if the maternal instinct does not "kick in" immediately just because you are pregnant.

  • Give it time: Give yourself a few days, maybe even a few weeks, to digest this news. Take a deep breath and do not rush to make decisions or plan the future.

Step 2: Medical confirmation and the first doctor's appointment

Although home tests are very accurate, it is important to consult a doctor to formalize the situation and ensure the pregnancy is developing healthily.

  • Blood test (HCG): Accurately confirms the pregnancy.

  • Ultrasound examination (USM): Essential for checking that the pregnancy is intrauterine (not ectopic) and for monitoring the fetal heartbeat.

  • Don't worry about the past: Many women feel terrible anxiety about a glass of wine they drank or medicine they took before they knew the news. Talk to your doctor; in most cases, small mistakes made at this early stage do not cause serious harm to the fetus.

Step 3: Talking to your partner (Spouse)

Sharing this news is one of the most nerve-wracking moments. The reaction may not always be like a movie scene.

  • Be prepared for shock: Like you, he may also need time to digest this news. Even if his first reaction is silence or confusion, it doesn't mean he doesn't want to be a father.

  • Open communication: Do not hide your fears (financial, career, etc.). You will go through this path together, and sharing your concerns will lighten your burden.

Step 4: Managing "Career and Plans" fears

An unplanned pregnancy often falls right in the middle of career goals, education, or travel plans.

  • Life doesn't stop: Pregnancy and motherhood are not the end of a career, just a new stage (sometimes a short break). Many successful women become more productive and focused on goals after motherhood.

  • Adapt your plans: Instead of erasing your goals, adapt them to the new reality. Instead of saying "I can never do this," say "I will do this at a slightly different time."

Step 5: Reviewing the financial situation

The question "Will we be able to take care of the child?" is one of the biggest sources of stress.

  • Budget planning: Write down your income and expenses. Make a list of items needed for the baby (often you need much less than you think).

  • State support: Research the one-time allowance (600 AZN) available in Azerbaijan, maternity leave, and other social assistance (See: Legal Aid section in the Anacan app).

Step 6: Transition to healthy habits

Once the shock passes, you should focus your attention on yourself and your baby.

  • Folic acid: If you haven't started yet, start immediately.

  • Nutrition and Sleep: Stress can weaken the immune system, so eating well and resting is now more important than ever.

The most beautiful adventures start unplanned

An unplanned child is not a guest who arrived "by mistake," but simply a gift that arrived a little early. Your life will definitely change, but this change will bring with it great love and meaning.

Give yourself time, don't hesitate to ask for support, and trust this miraculous process in your body.

Still confused?

Thousands of mothers like you have experienced these feelings. Download the Anacan app to join the "Mothers of the Same Month" group, read other women's stories, and feel that you are not alone on this journey.
