articles.title: 10 Foods to Avoid During Pregnancy: Sushi, Raw Meat, and Other Risks
articles.excerpt: What foods should you avoid during pregnancy? Why are sushi, raw eggs, soft cheeses, and liver dangerous? A list of 10 forbidden foods to protect against listeria and toxoplasmosis.
articles.content:
Pregnancy is the period when women most question their eating habits. On one hand, you think, "I crave it, so the baby needs it," and on the other, you fear, "Will eating this harm my baby?" Especially the richness of Azerbaijani cuisine and our love for natural village products can sometimes lead to hidden dangers.

Unfortunately, some of our favorite foods must be removed from the menu during pregnancy. The reason is simple: your immune system weakens slightly during pregnancy, and bacteria (Listeria, Salmonella) that wouldn't affect you normally can now pose a serious threat to your baby.

Let's take a look at 10 foods you should stay away from for 9 months and learn why they are on the "red list."

1. Raw Fish and Sushi (Sushi lovers, we're sorry!)

You may love Japanese cuisine, but it's essential to avoid rolls made with raw fish during pregnancy.

  • Danger: Raw fish can contain parasites and harmful bacteria.

  • Alternative: You can eat sushi that is fully cooked (e.g., "tempura" or cooked salmon) or made with vegetables (avocado, cucumber).

2. Raw or Undercooked Meat ("Bloody" Steak)

When eating kebabs or steaks, make sure the inside of the meat does not remain pink.

  • Danger: Risk of Toxoplasmosis infection. While this parasite isn't scary for adults, it can seriously damage the fetus's eyes and brain.

  • Rule: Meat must be fully cooked; no pink or bloody parts should remain.

3. Raw Eggs (Including village eggs!)

Sunny-side-up eggs at breakfast or homemade mayonnaise might be delicious, but they are risky.

  • Danger: Salmonella bacteria. This causes severe vomiting, diarrhea, and fever, which can lead to dehydration and uterine contractions.

  • Rule: Both the white and the yolk of the egg must be cooked until firm. "Gogol-mogol" or tasting raw dough is strictly forbidden.

4. High-Mercury Fish

Fish is a source of Omega-3, but you can't say "all fish are healthy." Some large fish accumulate mercury in the ocean.

  • Danger: Mercury can damage the developing nervous system and brain of the fetus.

  • Forbidden: Shark, swordfish, king mackerel.

  • Safe: Salmon, trout, sprat, sardines (2 portions per week).

5. Unpasteurized Milk and Soft Cheeses

The saying "village milk is natural and healthy" does not apply during pregnancy unless that milk has been boiled.

  • Danger: Listeria bacteria. This bacterium can cross the placenta and cause miscarriages or premature births.

  • What to avoid: Unboiled village milk and soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk (Brie, Camembert, Gorgonzola - moldy cheeses).

  • Safe: Boiled milk, pasteurized store-bought cheeses (white cheese, cheddar, Dutch cheese).

6. Unwashed Fruits and Vegetables

Even the healthiest apple is a source of danger if not washed.

  • Danger: Toxoplasmosis parasite transmitted from the soil.

  • Rule: Wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running water. When ordering salads in restaurants, ensure they are clean (or choose cooked vegetables).

7. Liver

Although liver is a source of iron, one must be careful during pregnancy.

  • Danger: It contains very high amounts of Vitamin A (Retinol). Excess Vitamin A can cause fetal developmental defects.

  • Advice: Do not eat it more than 1-2 times a month.

8. Processed Meats (Sausages, Hot Dogs)

If you love sausages for breakfast, be careful.

  • Danger: Risk of Listeria. Even if these products are sold cooked, bacteria can be introduced during packaging.

  • Rule: Be sure to fry or cook sausages and hot dogs until they are "steaming hot" (thoroughly). Do not eat them cold.

9. Alcohol

This is the strictest prohibition. The idea that "one glass of wine won't hurt" is wrong.

  • Danger: Alcohol passes directly into the baby's blood and can cause Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (physical and mental defects). There is NO safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy.

10. Excessive Caffeine

You don't have to cut out coffee entirely, but you should reduce it.

  • Limit: Daily 200 mg (about 1-2 cups).

  • Risk: High amounts of caffeine increase the risk of miscarriage and can reduce the baby's birth weight. Remember that tea, chocolate, and cola also contain caffeine.

Don't let this list scare you. In fact, the number of delicious and healthy foods you can eat far outweighs the forbidden ones. The main logic is cleanliness and cooking. If you are sure the food is washed clean and fully cooked, the risk is minimal.

If you have doubts about any food, check the "Safety Lookup" in the Anacan app. You can instantly check the status (Green/Yellow/Red) of hundreds of foods there.

Eat healthy, raise a healthy baby!

articles.title: Sex During Pregnancy: When Is It Safe and When to Avoid?
articles.excerpt: Does sex during pregnancy harm the baby? In which cases is sex prohibited? Everything you need to know about libido changes, safety rules, and situations where doctors say "stop."
articles.content:
After receiving the news of pregnancy, one of the first questions that comes to couples' minds, but which they are most ashamed to ask the doctor, is this: "Can our sex life continue, or will it harm the baby?"

There are so many myths and fears surrounding this topic that many couples distance themselves from each other for 9 months. Some fear the baby will "feel" them, while others worry about injury. Let's break these taboos and clarify when sexual intercourse during pregnancy is safe and when it is risky, based on medical facts.

The main question: Does it harm the baby?

Short answer: No.

If your pregnancy is proceeding normally and no specific restrictions have been set by your doctor, sexual intercourse is completely safe for your baby.

Your baby is inside a very secure "fortress" in the mother's womb:

  • Amniotic fluid: Acts as a "cushion" protecting the baby from impacts.

  • Uterine muscles: Strong walls surround the baby.

  • Mucus plug: Seals the cervix, preventing infections from entering.

Myth: "The baby knows or feels what is happening during intercourse."

Truth: The baby does not understand what is happening. They may only feel an increase in the mother's heart rate and a slight rocking motion, as if in a cradle.

>

Pregnancy trimesters and sexual desire (Libido)

It is normal for your sexual desire to rise and fall like a "roller coaster" throughout pregnancy.

  • 1st Trimester (Fatigue period): Sexual desire may decrease due to nausea (morning sickness), weakness, and breast tenderness. During this period, many women simply want to sleep.

  • 2nd Trimester (Honeymoon): Your energy returns, and nausea passes. Due to increased blood flow to the pelvic organs, many women experience higher libido and more intense sensations during this period.

  • 3rd Trimester (Search for comfort): As the belly grows, movement becomes difficult and back pain occurs. Sexual desire may decrease again, but this does not apply to everyone.

When to say "NO"? (Medical Contraindications)

In some cases, your doctor may prescribe "pelvic rest". These are instances where sexual intercourse and even orgasm are prohibited:

1. Risk of miscarriage or bleeding

If you are in the early stages of pregnancy and have unexplained vaginal bleeding, spotting, or severe cramps, your doctor will prohibit sexual intercourse until the situation stabilizes.

2. Placenta Previa (Low-lying placenta)

This is when the placenta is located low and covers the cervix completely or partially. Sexual intercourse can cause serious bleeding. If this diagnosis is made, sexual intercourse is strictly prohibited until delivery.

3. Cervical insufficiency (Incompetent cervix)

If the cervix shortens or opens prematurely, sexual intercourse can trigger preterm labor.

4. Risk of premature birth

If you have had a premature birth in previous pregnancies or if your contractions have started early in this pregnancy, caution is necessary. The prostaglandins in semen can soften the cervix and accelerate labor.

5. Rupture of membranes (Water breaking)

If your water has broken or there is a leak, it means the barrier protecting the baby has been breached. In this case, sexual intercourse poses a serious risk of infection.

Frequently asked concerns

"There was bleeding after intercourse, is this normal?"

During pregnancy, the cervix is better supplied with blood and becomes more sensitive. Light, pink spotting after intercourse can be considered normal. However, if the bleeding is like a menstrual period or is accompanied by pain, consult a doctor immediately.

"Does orgasm start labor?"

In a normal pregnancy, uterine contractions (Braxton Hicks) that occur during orgasm are harmless and pass quickly. However, in the final days of pregnancy (closer to the 40th week), some doctors recommend sexual intercourse to start labor naturally (due to the softening effect of semen).

Tips for Safety and Comfort

  • Positions: As your belly grows, face-to-face positions may become uncomfortable. The "spooning" (side-lying) position or positions where the woman is on top are more comfortable as they do not put pressure on the belly.

  • Avoid lying on your back: After the 20th week, lying on your back can compress the "inferior vena cava," which can cause dizziness and reduce blood flow to the baby.

  • Communication: Tell your partner and stop if you feel any discomfort or pain.

Pregnancy is a special period where feelings of femininity and motherhood combine. Sexual life is a natural part of this period, and if there is no medical prohibition, there is no need to give it up. On the contrary, it can strengthen your emotional bond with your partner.

If you have doubts, do not hesitate to consult your doctor. And remember, intimacy is not just about sexual intercourse—hugging, massaging, and spending time together are also ways to show your love.

Note: If you feel any unusual symptoms related to your pregnancy (pain, bleeding, water leaking), record them in the Anacan app and contact your doctor immediately.

articles.title: What is Ectopic Pregnancy? Symptoms and Risk Factors
articles.excerpt: What is ectopic (extrauterine) pregnancy and how does it occur? Learn about abdominal pain, bleeding, and other hidden danger signs. Everything you need to know to reduce risks and protect your chances for future pregnancy.
articles.content:
The news of pregnancy should be a moment full of joy for every woman. However, sometimes those two lines on a pregnancy test can bring anxiety instead of happiness. According to medical statistics, approximately 1-2% of all pregnancies result in an ectopic (extrauterine) pregnancy.

This diagnosis may sound scary, but early intervention saves lives and preserves your chances of becoming a mother in the future. So, how can you distinguish an ectopic pregnancy from a normal one? Which pains should be considered "alarm signals"? Let's explore this important topic together.

What exactly is an ectopic pregnancy?

In a normal pregnancy, the fertilized egg cell passes through the fallopian tubes, reaches the uterus (womb), and begins to develop there.

In an ectopic pregnancy, the fertilized egg cannot reach the uterus and gets stuck somewhere along the way—most commonly in the fallopian tubes (98%)—where it attaches. That is why it is colloquially known as a "tubal pregnancy." In very rare cases, it can also occur in the ovaries, abdominal cavity, or cervix.

The bitter truth: Unfortunately, it is impossible for a fetus to survive and develop outside the uterus. The growth of these tissues can cause the tube to burst, leading to internal bleeding that poses a life-threatening risk to the mother.

>

Hidden Danger: How to recognize the symptoms?

The most confusing part of an ectopic pregnancy is that, at first, it looks exactly like a normal pregnancy. Your period is late, the test is positive, and there may even be nausea and breast tenderness.

However, between the 4th and 10th weeks of pregnancy, the following "red flag" symptoms may appear:

1. Sharp abdominal or pelvic pain

Mild cramps can occur in a normal pregnancy, but the pain in an ectopic pregnancy is different:

  • Usually, there is a sharp, stabbing pain on only one side of the abdomen (right or left).

  • The pain may come and go or be constant.

2. Abnormal vaginal bleeding

This bleeding differs from a normal menstrual period.

  • It is often lighter in amount, brownish in color, or watery.

  • Sometimes women mistake this for a late period and do not realize they are pregnant.

3. Shoulder tip pain (Special symptom)

Although this sounds very strange, it is one of the most serious signs of an ectopic pregnancy. If you feel pain at the tip of your shoulder (where the arm meets the body) while lying down, it may indicate that internal bleeding is irritating the diaphragm. Seek emergency medical attention immediately.

4. Weakness and dizziness

Internal bleeding can cause a drop in blood pressure, paleness, and fainting.

Risks: Why does this happen?

Any woman can encounter this situation, but certain factors increase the risk:

  • Previous ectopic pregnancy: If you have experienced this before, the chance of recurrence is slightly higher.

  • Inflammatory diseases and infections: Sexually transmitted infections (chlamydia, gonorrhea) cause inflammation and scarring in the fallopian tubes, obstructing the egg's movement.

  • Tubal surgery: If you have previously had any surgery on your tubes.

  • Smoking: Research shows that smoking reduces the motility of the fallopian tubes.

  • In vitro fertilization (IVF): Although rare, the risk increases slightly.

  • Age: The risk is higher in women over 35 years of age.

Diagnosis and Treatment

If you suspect an ectopic pregnancy, there is no time to lose. Your doctor will use two methods to confirm the diagnosis:

  • Blood test (Beta-HCG): In an ectopic pregnancy, the HCG hormone increases more slowly than in a normal pregnancy or fluctuates.

  • Ultrasound examination (USG): If the test is positive but no gestational sac is visible inside the uterus, the doctor will check the tubes.

Treatment methods:

  • Medical treatment (Methotrexate): If the pregnancy is very small and the tube has not burst, the pregnancy is terminated with a special injection, and the body absorbs the tissue. This is the best way to preserve the tube.

  • Surgery (Laparoscopy): If the fetus is large or there is internal bleeding, surgery is performed through small incisions. Depending on the situation, the tube may be preserved or removed.

Can I become a mother after an ectopic pregnancy?

This is the most frequently asked and most important question. The answer: Yes!

The vast majority of women have a normal, healthy pregnancy and become mothers after an ectopic pregnancy. Even if one tube is removed, if the other tube is healthy, your chances of conceiving naturally remain high.

Simply, the next time you become pregnant, your doctor will monitor you more closely and schedule an early ultrasound (around the 6th week) to ensure the sac has reached the uterus.

An ectopic pregnancy is a physically and emotionally difficult trial. Give yourself time to grieve and heal. Always pay attention to the signals your body gives you.

Remember, early diagnosis protects not only your health but also your future chances of motherhood. If you are planning a pregnancy or are already pregnant, record your symptoms in the Anacan app and contact your doctor immediately regarding any suspicious points.

articles.title: Fetal Development: What Happens to Your Baby and Your Body in the 1st Trimester?
articles.excerpt: How does your baby develop in the first 12 weeks (1st trimester) of pregnancy? When can you hear the heartbeat? Learn everything about the changes in the mother's body and the miraculous journey from a single cell to a human.
articles.content:
The moment you see those two lines on a pregnancy test is one of the most unforgettable moments of your life. Joy, excitement, and perhaps a little fear... All these feelings are completely normal. You may not have changed outwardly yet, but the greatest miracle of the universe is happening inside you: a new life is being created.

The first three months of pregnancy, i.e., the 1st trimester, is the most critical and rapid period for the baby's development. In just 12 weeks, a single invisible cell transforms into a miniature human with a beating heart, arms, and legs. Let's take a closer look at what happens to both your baby and your body during this magical period.

What is the 1st Trimester? (Weeks 1-12)

Pregnancy is divided into three stages (trimesters). The first trimester begins on the first day of your last period and lasts until the end of the 12th week. This period is the most important stage in terms of the formation of the baby's organs ("organogenesis"). That is why a healthy lifestyle and nutrition play a decisive role in the first months.

How is your baby changing? From a microscopic particle to a "plum-sized" baby

Month 1: Laying the Foundation (Weeks 1-4)

In the first two weeks of pregnancy, you are technically not pregnant yet (your body is preparing for ovulation). The real adventure begins after fertilization occurs.

  • From Zygote to Blastocyst: The fertilized egg cell (zygote) divides rapidly, moves toward the uterus, and attaches to the uterine wall (implantation).

  • Size: At the end of the month, your baby is the size of a poppy seed.

  • Key Development: The neural tube, which forms the basis of the baby's brain and spinal cord, begins to form. (See: Why is folic acid important?).

Month 2: The heart starts beating! (Weeks 5-8)

This month is the most active period of development. Your baby is now called an "embryo."

  • Heart: At approximately the 6th week, the baby's heart begins to beat! This can be heard on an USG (Ultrasound Examination). The heart works very fast at 100-160 beats per minute.

  • Facial Features: Eyes, ears, and nose begin to form.

  • Limbs: Arms and legs first appear as small buds, and by the end of the month, fingers begin to be seen.

  • Size: At 8 weeks, your baby is about the size of a raspberry or a kidney bean.

Month 3: Human Form (Weeks 9-12)

The "embryo" stage is now over, and your baby begins to be called a "fetus."

  • Movement: The baby begins to move, but you don't feel it yet (there's still time for that!).

  • Organs: All major organs (kidneys, intestines, brain) have formed and begun to function. Fingernails appear.

  • Gender: Genitals are forming, but it may still be too early to see on an ultrasound.

  • Size: At the end of the trimester, your baby is the size of a lemon or a plum (approximately 5-6 cm).

So, What is Happening in Your Body?

While your baby is growing rapidly, a "hormone storm" is occurring in your body. Although nothing is apparent from the outside yet, serious work is going on inside.

1. Fatigue and Weakness

Do you constantly feel sleepy? This is due to the increase in the hormone progesterone. Your body spends a lot of energy to create the placenta. Be kind to yourself and rest as much as possible.

2. Morning Sickness (Toxemia)

Approximately 70% of pregnant women encounter this condition. Nausea can occur at any time of the day. Extreme sensitivity to smells is also a "travel companion" of this period. (Good news: These conditions usually pass in the second trimester).

3. Breast Sensitivity

Your breasts may grow, become heavy, and be very sensitive to touch. Mammary glands are already preparing for lactation.

4. Frequent Urination

The growing uterus presses on the bladder, and increased blood circulation causes the kidneys to work more.

5. Emotional Fluctuations (Mood Swings)

It is completely normal to laugh one moment and cry the next. Hormones change brain chemistry.

Important Tips for the 1st Trimester

What should you pay attention to in order to spend this critical period healthily?

  • Don't forget vitamins: Take Folic acid or prenatal vitamins prescribed by your doctor every day.

  • Say goodbye to harmful habits: Smoking (including passive smoking) and alcohol directly harm the baby's development.

  • Pay attention to nutrition: Stay away from raw meat, raw eggs, unpasteurized dairy products, and high-mercury fish.

  • Doctor's appointment: Go for your first gynecological examination. Hearing the baby's heartbeat will give you great motivation.

  • Drink water: Fluid loss is high during toxemia, so try to drink plenty of water.

The first trimester is one of the most difficult yet most miraculous periods of pregnancy. Changes in your body may tire you out, but remember that every symptom is a sign that your baby is growing.

articles.title: Preparing for Pregnancy: Why Is Folic Acid So Important?
articles.excerpt: Planning to get pregnant? Find out why folic acid (Vitamin B9) should be your first step and learn when and how much you should take to protect your baby from developmental defects.
articles.content:
If you have decided to get pregnant, you have probably already started dreaming about your future baby, perhaps even thinking about colors for the nursery. However, the first and perhaps most important step you will take to have a healthy baby is not choosing a stroller, but going to the pharmacy to buy Folic Acid.

So why is this small vitamin considered the "gold standard" of pregnancy planning? Why do doctors call it "baby insurance"? Let's talk about the miraculous effects and usage rules of folic acid.

What is folic acid (Vitamin B9) actually?

Folic acid is the synthetic form of Vitamin B9, one of the B group vitamins (the form found naturally in food is called "folate"). This vitamin is of vital importance for the creation of new cells and the formation of DNA in our bodies.

From the first moment a baby enters the mother's womb, it consists of rapidly dividing cells. The body needs a large amount of folic acid specifically for this division process to proceed correctly.

Why should I start specifically "before pregnancy"?

Many women start taking vitamins after learning they are pregnant. This is, of course, beneficial, but the most critical moment is often missed.

1. Prevention of neural tube defects

The neural tube, which forms the basis of the baby's brain and spinal column, forms and closes within the first 28 days of pregnancy. During this period, you may not even know you are pregnant yet.

If there is a folic acid deficiency in the body, the neural tube may not close completely. This can cause serious birth defects such as Spina Bifida (cleft spine) or Anencephaly (brain development disorder). Research shows that folic acid taken on time reduces these risks by up to 70%.

2. Reduction of miscarriage risk

Healthy DNA production helps the embryo attach firmly to the uterine wall and develop in the early stages of pregnancy. Vitamin B9 deficiency is associated with early miscarriages.

3. Prevention of anemia

Blood volume increases during pregnancy. Folic acid protects both the mother and the baby from anemia by participating in the production of red blood cells.

How much and when should it be taken?

The recommendation of the World Health Organization and gynecologists is clear:

  • Timing: It is necessary to start at least 1-3 months before trying to get pregnant and continue throughout the first 12 weeks of pregnancy (first trimester).

  • Dosage: A daily intake of 400 mcg (micrograms) of folic acid is standardly recommended.

Attention: If there has been a child born with nervous system defects in your family, if you have diabetes, or if you take epilepsy medications, your doctor may prescribe a higher dose (e.g., 5 mg) for you. Do not take high doses on your own.

>

Natural foods or pills?

The question "I eat healthy, do I need medicine?" is often asked. Unfortunately, it is difficult to collect the required amount through food alone, because a large part of folates is destroyed during cooking. However, it is essential to enrich your diet.

Foods richest in folic acid:

  • Green leafy vegetables: Spinach, lettuce, broccoli.

  • Legumes: Lentils, chickpeas, beans (you are lucky because these are abundant in Azerbaijani cuisine!).

  • Citrus fruits: Orange, lemon, tangerine.

  • Walnuts and hazelnuts.

  • Liver (However, it should be limited during pregnancy due to high Vitamin A content).

Conclusion

Preparing for pregnancy is not just about financial and spiritual readiness, but also preparing your body for this miracle. Taking folic acid is the easiest and most effective investment you can make for the health of your future child.

From today, make it a habit to take a small vitamin with a glass of water. Remember, a healthy mother means a healthy future.

articles.title: How to Calculate Ovulation Day: Methods to Increase Your Chances of Getting Pregnant
articles.excerpt: How to calculate your ovulation day to increase your chances of getting pregnant? A detailed guide on the calendar method, basal body temperature, cervical mucus, and ovulation tests.
articles.content:
When planning a pregnancy, the question "why isn't it happening yet?" can become a source of stress for many couples. In reality, even for healthy couples, it can take several months to achieve pregnancy. The main secret here is "correct timing".

A woman's body is capable of becoming pregnant only a few days a month (approximately 5-6 days). This period is called the "fertile window," and its peak is the ovulation day. So, how can you catch this golden day? Let's learn how to calculate ovulation using scientific and natural methods.

What is ovulation and when does it occur?

Ovulation is the process where a mature egg cell is released from the ovary and enters the fallopian tube. At this time, the egg is ready to meet a sperm and be fertilized.

  • Short lifespan: The egg cell lives for only 12-24 hours. If fertilization does not occur during this period, it dies.

  • Strength of sperm: Sperm can live in a woman's body for up to 3-5 days.

  • Result: The highest chance of pregnancy occurs during sexual intercourse 3 days before ovulation and on the day of ovulation itself.

Myth: "Ovulation always happens on the 14th day, right in the middle of the cycle."

Truth: This is only for women with an ideal 28-day cycle. Every woman's cycle is different, and the ovulation day can vary.

>

4 main methods to calculate ovulation

1. Calendar method (Simplest, but least accurate)

This method works if your menstrual cycle is regular.

  • Formula: Ovulation usually occurs 14 days before the start of the next period.

  • Example: If your cycle is 30 days: 30 - 14 = 16. This means ovulation occurs approximately on the 16th day.

  • Anacan help: Don't waste time calculating by hand. Simply record the first day of your last period in the Anacan app, and the smart algorithm will calculate the fertile days for you.

2. Ovulation tests (Most accurate home method)

These tests, sold in pharmacies, are similar to pregnancy tests but look for a different hormone: Luteinizing Hormone (LH). LH levels rise sharply 24-36 hours before ovulation.

  • How to use: During the approximate ovulation week, take a urine test every day at the same time (preferably in the afternoon). If you see two dark lines, ovulation will occur within the next 24 hours. This is the most ideal time for intercourse!

3. Basal Body Temperature (BBT)

This method requires patience and discipline, but it is excellent for getting to know your body.

  • Rule: Measure your temperature every morning before getting out of bed and without making any movement (even drinking water).

  • Sign: Immediately after ovulation, your temperature rises by approximately 0.3 - 0.5 degrees due to the effect of the progesterone hormone and remains high until your period.

  • Note: This method shows that ovulation has occurred (it might already be late), but after tracking for a few months, you will find your own pattern.

4. Cervical mucus (Discharge) method

Your body gives you the clearest sign in your underwear.

  • Dry period: Immediately after menstruation.

  • Sticky: As ovulation approaches.

  • Like "egg white": On the day of ovulation, the discharge becomes clear, slippery, and stretchy (you can stretch it between your fingers). This fluid facilitates the movement of sperm and indicates the most fertile period.

Additional tips to increase the chance of getting pregnant

In addition to calculating the right day, small changes you make in your lifestyle can also make a big difference:

  • Reduce stress: Cortisol (the stress hormone) can delay or completely stop ovulation. Yoga, meditation, or simply doing what you love will protect your hormonal balance.

  • Healthy weight: Both excess weight and being underweight affect hormones.

  • Nutrition: Stay away from trans fats, increase plant-based proteins (lentils, chickpeas), and don't forget folic acid intake.

  • Quit smoking: Smoking reduces ovarian reserve and worsens egg quality.

When to see a doctor?

  • If you are under 35 and pregnancy has not occurred despite 1 year of regular attempts.

  • If you are over 35 and there is no result within 6 months.

  • If your periods are very irregular (or absent altogether).

Knowing your ovulation day is your compass on the road to pregnancy. Learn your body's language, track the symptoms, but don't turn the process into a mechanical task. Maintaining a sense of love and intimacy is just as important as the result of an LH test.

articles.title: When Should You Take a Pregnancy Test? Golden Rules for Accurate Results
articles.excerpt: When should you take a pregnancy test? Should I wait for a missed period or can I check earlier? Everything you need to know about the best time of day for accurate results and the hCG hormone.
articles.content:
When you are trying to get pregnant or suspect you might be, "waiting" can seem like the hardest job in the world. Every time you enter a pharmacy, you look at those little boxes on the shelf and think, "maybe I should check now?" However, rushing can often lead to disappointment – a "false negative" result or unnecessary stress.

But when is the ideal time to see those two magic lines? Does it matter whether you take the test in the morning or evening? In this article, we have gathered all the truths about pregnancy tests to save your money and your nerves.

How do pregnancy tests work? (hCG Hormone)

To understand when a test should be taken, you first need to know what it is looking for. All home pregnancy tests work by detecting a specific hormone in the urine called hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin).

  • Process: After a fertilized egg attaches to the uterine wall (implantation), the placenta begins to secrete this hormone.

  • Duration: hCG levels double every 2-3 days. However, the hormone must reach a certain concentration for the test to be able to "see" it.

If you take the test too early, even if you are pregnant, the hCG level may not have reached the test's sensitivity threshold yet. Result? One line and unnecessary sadness.

The right time to take the test

The main rule here is to be patient. Two main approaches exist:

1. Most accurate result: After a missed period

Most doctors and test manufacturers recommend waiting for a missed period (at least 1 day past the expected date).

  • Reason: During this period, hCG levels in most women reach a level that standard tests can detect. At this time, the accuracy of tests is close to 99%.

2. For the impatient: Before the delay (Early tests)

Some "Early Detection" tests claim to show results 4-5 days before your period. These tests are more sensitive (they catch hCG at lower amounts).

  • Risk: If you get a negative result, it does not mean you are not pregnant. It might just be too early. In this case, you should check again a few days later.

What time of day is better? Morning or Evening?

The idea that "you must take the test in the morning" is not just a myth, but a recommendation with a scientific basis.

  • First morning urine: Because it has collected overnight, it has the highest concentration. The hCG hormone is most dense here. Taking a morning test is essential in the early stages (before a delay or on the day of the delay).

  • Afternoon and Evening: If your period is already 1-2 weeks late, the hCG level is so high that you can take the test at any time of day.

Important note: Drinking excessive water or tea before the test dilutes the urine and reduces the hCG concentration. This can lead to a false negative result.

>

False Negative and False Positive results

Sometimes tests can deceive us. It is important to know the reasons for this:

False Negative (You are pregnant, but the test says "no")

  • Reason 1: You took the test too early (the most common reason).

  • Reason 2: The urine was too diluted (you drank too much water).

  • Reason 3: The test has expired.

False Positive (You are not pregnant, but the test says "yes")

This is much rarer, but possible:

  • Chemical pregnancy: Fertilization occurred, but the embryo did not develop.

  • Evaporation line: A faint, gray-colored line that appears after the time given to check the test (usually 5-10 minutes) has passed. This is not a positive result.

  • Certain medications: Infertility drugs containing hCG can affect the result.

When should a blood test (hCG) be given?

If home tests have confused you or you want a more accurate result, a blood test is the most reliable way.

  • A blood test detects hCG earlier (7-10 days after fertilization) and more accurately than a urine test.

  • This analysis also shows the exact amount of the hormone (beta-hCG), allowing you to track which week of pregnancy you are in and whether development is proceeding normally.

5 Golden Rules for an Accurate Result

When using a home pregnancy test, be sure to follow these steps:

  • Check the date: Always check the expiration date when buying a test. Old tests give incorrect results.

  • Read the instructions: Rules may differ for every brand (e.g., the duration it should stay in the urine).

  • Wait for the morning: For the most accurate result, use the first urine as soon as you wake up in the morning.

  • Keep time: Look at the result within the time interval indicated in the instructions (e.g., after 3-5 minutes). Do not believe lines that appear after 10 minutes.

  • Repeat: If the result is negative but your period still hasn't come, repeat the test 2-3 days later.

Taking a pregnancy test is an exciting moment, and waiting for the result can feel like an eternity. The best strategy is to give nature a little time and at least wait for the day of your period.

If the result is positive, congratulations! A wonderful journey awaits you. Now the next step is to book a doctor's appointment and download the Anacan app to track your baby's development week by week. If the result is negative, don't lose heart; maybe it's just still too early.

articles.title: Early Signs of Pregnancy: How to Tell if You Are Pregnant Without a Test
articles.excerpt: How can you feel that you are pregnant before a missed period? A detailed guide on early pregnancy symptoms, implantation bleeding, basal body temperature, and the hidden signals your body gives.
articles.content:
"Am I pregnant?" — this question is probably the most exciting and perhaps the most frightening question crossing your mind right now. It is still too early to buy a pregnancy test from the pharmacy, or maybe you just don't have the patience to wait for the result. As you approach the end of each menstrual cycle, you begin to monitor every small change in your body: "Is this just fatigue, or is it a sign?"

Fortunately, your body begins to give you certain signals long before the test shows the result. Hormonal changes kick in immediately after fertilization. In this article, we have researched for you the ways to feel pregnancy without testing, the earliest symptoms, and how you can distinguish pregnancy signs from PMS (premenstrual syndrome).

What happens in your body before a missed period?

For many women, the first obvious sign of pregnancy is a missed period. However, if you are careful, your body can "send you news" even before that. In the first weeks of pregnancy (in medical terms, weeks 3-4 calculated from the first day of the last period), the increase in progesterone and HCG hormones causes a series of physiological changes.

Implantation bleeding and spotting

About 6-12 days after fertilization, the embryo attaches to the uterine wall. During this process, some women observe light pink or brown spotting. In medicine, this is called implantation bleeding.

  • How to tell the difference? This bleeding is much less than a normal period, lasts for a short time (sometimes a few hours), and is usually painless. If you see just a few drops of spots on your underwear, this could be the first "hello" of pregnancy.

Basal temperature staying high

If you measure your basal temperature every morning to track ovulation, your graph can give you the most accurate clue. Normally, the temperature rises after ovulation and drops as the period approaches.

  • Pregnancy sign: If your temperature continues to stay high for more than 2 weeks and does not drop, this most likely indicates pregnancy.

Most common early pregnancy symptoms

In the first days after a delay or even before it, the following signs show themselves more prominently. Not every woman may experience all of these symptoms, but the most common ones are:

Breast sensitivity and enlargement

One of the earliest and most common signs of pregnancy is changes in the breasts. Under the influence of hormones, the mammary glands become swollen, heavy, and extremely sensitive to touch.

  • What will you feel? The color of the nipples (areola) may darken and the veins may appear more prominent. This feeling is usually sharper than the pain experienced during PMS.

Unexplained fatigue and weakness

Are you having trouble waking up in the morning? Do your eyes close during the afternoon? The sharp increase in the progesterone hormone puts you into a sort of "sleep mode." Your body spends great energy to create a new life, blood sugar and blood pressure may drop, which can make you feel constantly tired.

Morning sickness (Toxicosis)

Although it is called "morning," it can happen at any time of the day — morning, afternoon, or night. For some women, this is just mild nausea, while for others it is a difficult process accompanied by vomiting. Although it starts in the 4th-6th weeks of pregnancy, it can be felt earlier in some sensitive organisms.

Acute sensitivity to odors

Does the smell of your favorite perfume now seem unbearable to you? Or do you feel the smell of the food the neighbor is cooking in your home? The increase in the estrogen hormone raises your sense of smell to a "superpower" level. This is often directly related to loss of appetite and nausea.

Frequent urination

During pregnancy, the amount of blood in your body increases, which causes the kidneys to process more fluid. As a result, your need to go to the toilet increases significantly. Although this symptom usually starts after the 6th week, it is observed earlier in some women due to hormonal changes.

Psychological changes: "Mood Swings"

One minute ago you were laughing, and now you want to cry for no reason? Pregnancy hormones affect your brain's neurotransmitters, causing emotional fluctuations. Although this is similar to the PMS period, emotions are sharper and more sudden in pregnancy. It is completely normal to feel irritable, fragile, or excessively anxious.

PMS or Pregnancy? How to know the difference?

Pregnancy signs and premenstrual syndrome (PMS) are often confused. Here are the main differences:

  • Bleeding: Does not occur in PMS; there may be short-term "implantation bleeding" in pregnancy.

  • Appetite: In PMS, the desire for sweets and salty foods increases, while in pregnancy, a sharp repulsion from certain foods (e.g., meat or eggs) may occur.

  • Abdominal pain: PMS pains are more severe, while in early pregnancy, there is a feeling of light stretching or stinging.

Is it possible to be 100% sure without testing?

Short answer: No.

All the signs listed above — fatigue, breast pain, even a delay — can also arise from other causes (stress, hormonal disorder, seasonal change, travel). Some women do not feel any symptoms in the early period even if they are pregnant.

The signals your body gives you just provide a strong "clue." The only scientific way to confirm your suspicions is a pregnancy test.

  • Home tests (Urine test): Gives more accurate results 1-2 days after a missed period.

  • Blood test (HCG): Shows the most accurate result 7-10 days after fertilization, i.e., even before a missed period.

Early pregnancy signs can be different for every woman, and even in different pregnancies of the same woman. If you feel the listed symptoms in yourself:

  • Be calm: Stress hormones can negatively affect your body.

  • Pay attention to your nutrition: Stay away from alcohol and start taking folic acid.

  • Start tracking: Use the Anacan app to record your symptoms. The smart tracker in our app will help you understand whether the changes in your body are normal.

If your period is delayed or if the symptoms worsen, definitely consult your doctor. Remember, every new feeling brings you one step closer to the big meeting.

Your privacy is important to us. This privacy policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal information when you use the Anacan app.

1. Information We Collect

When you use the Anacan app, we may collect personal information such as your name, email address, and usage data.

2. How We Use Information

Your information is used to provide, improve, and personalize our services, as well as to communicate with you.

3. Data Security

We implement strict security measures to protect your information. Your data is encrypted and stored on secure servers.

4. Third-Party Services

We do not sell your information. We may use trusted third-party services that meet strict privacy standards.

5. Your Rights

You have the right to access, modify, or delete your personal information at any time through your account settings.

Advertising, AdMob, and Device Identifiers

We may use Google AdMob to display ads in the Anacan app. AdMob and its third-party advertising partners may collect, use, and share device identifiers and related technical information to display and tailor ads, limit the number of times you see the same ad, measure ad performance, ensure security, and prevent fraud.

Information that may be collected

  • Android Advertising ID, iOS Advertising Identifier (IDFA — only when required permission is granted), and similar identifiers;
  • IP address, device model, language, time zone, mobile operator, operating system, and app version;
  • app usage, ad views, clicks, ad interactions, and diagnostic information;
  • approximate location derivable from the IP address. Precise location for advertising may only be used with separate permission and if such a function exists in the app.

Ad Personalization and Legal Basis

With your consent and where permitted by the laws of your country of residence, this information may be used for personalized ads tailored to your interests. If you do not consent or withdraw your consent, non-personalized or restricted ads may be shown. Such ads may still use limited information such as device data, app content, approximate location, and ad interaction. Data processing may be based on consent, service provision, or legitimate interests, in accordance with applicable legislation.

Your Choices on iOS Devices

In accordance with Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) guidelines, your permission may be requested before accessing IDFA for tracking across apps and websites. Not granting permission does not prevent you from using the app's core functions. You can change your choice at any time in iPhone or iPad Settings → Privacy & Security → Tracking.

Your Choices on Android Devices

Depending on your Android device version, you can manage ad personalization options, reset or delete your advertising identifier in Settings → Privacy → Ads. You can also manage your Google account ad preferences via My Ad Center. Menu names may vary depending on the device manufacturer and Android version.

Third Parties, Storage, and Transfer

Google and its advertising partners process data in accordance with their privacy policies, and data may be transferred to servers located outside your country of residence. The retention period depends on the type of data, advertising purpose, legal requirements, and the policies of the respective party. Anacan does not control the independent data processing of third parties. For users considered children by law, personalized ads are restricted, and applicable age-appropriate advertising guidelines are taken into account.

More Information and Options

  • Google Privacy & Terms
  • Google Ad Partners
  • Google My Ad Center

For questions about ad data processing and your privacy choices, you can write to privacy@anacan.az.
